title: Funding - Asset Diversification proposal_Fund A
body:
_**15th February 2022**_

Advait, VismayJoshi, Ash
Discord: Advait#5627, Vismay Joshi#6445, ash|inthewild#2521

**PURPOSE:**
The purpose of this proposal is to found the financial working group consisting of Advait, Vismay and Ash to request $11,000 in EDG (market equivalent) for investment purposes on behalf of Edgeware’s community Treasury into other blockchain assets (tokens). The funds are to be used to create a diversified portfolio of blockchain assets (tokens) that appreciate in value (monetary, utility) overtime that Edgeware can use for capital heavy opex (operating expense) or funding future growth.

- Requesting: $11,000 in EDG equivalent (as per 7 day average)
- Team members: Advait, Vismay, Ash
- Expected return on investment: 15-20 % 
- Fees: 10-20 
- 10%- fees for management 
- 20% - profit allocation to be paid as productivity bounty.
- Timeline: 2-12-22 to 2-12-23


	                                                      **–TLDR–**

**PROBLEM:**

We believe the problem is twofold:

1.   The Edgeware token(s) monetary value is volatile.
2.   The Edgeware token(s) monetary value is diminishing.

The reasons for these problems are due to an exceedingly competitive marketplace of blockchain projects, a lack of awareness to retail investors and an unknown/confusing use-case. It is to be noted that there are other factors beyond the project such as industry trends in project types, capital and regulation that have also added to the volatility and dampened price.

**SOLUTION:**
Our solution is to seek an allocation of tokens from Edgeware’s Treasury and invest it into a diverse set of blockchain assets; this will result in limiting our exposure to a single volatile asset/ecosystem. This approach also allows the Treasury to have a basket of assets that are diverse and appreciate in value across a period of time w/ sound investment strategies.
The investment approach also allows for the Treasury at a future point to utilize the yield generated from the assets

## Statement

The Edgeware Agency was formed from a set of community volunteers interested in earning EDG to tackle high-priority network issues. We are now at the end of the funds provided by the first proposal, posted 10 months ago in May. In order to continue operations, we require more funds to be allocated asap. 

The agency is at an awkward point: We are developing new patterns and tools for permissionless contribution, testing bounties, and our volunteers have grown in their expertise so as to become councilmembers of EDG, or are otherwise self-sufficient. If Edgeware is an ashram, the Agency has been the daily practice hall, and I’ve been honored to support and test the growth and character of our most core contributors. 

However, one of our goals was to decentralize ourselves using tools and that individual growth. I have asked that the top performers proceed with drafts of their own funding proposals, reflecting my belief that they no longer need my intermediary oversight and can benefit from directly interfacing with the community.

I believe that we should proceed with more intense focus on marketing, staking participation, and governance participation, however, with decentralization comes a loss of execution speed. That said, we basically estimated our progress successfully according to Proposal 1’s deliverables (at top.) title: [Proposal] Market Maker-faciliatated Liquidation and Exchange B Final Items
body:
# Intro


This proposal follows weeks of discussion in our Tuesday financial calls, whose meeting notes and recordings you can peruse at the [Financial Calls recorded.](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1YKHHV7cNuCaYGNHs5esFQsEPxtB-shM4)

This WG is in general agreement to move forward with a proposal to run a slow, bot-managed liquidation of EDG on Kucoin in order to complete the previously approved **[Proposal to list on Exchange B](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/1004-proposal-exchange-b-edg )**, and I've also included a purchase of extra BTC for market-making on Kucoin, explained below.

## Problem

1. In order to complete our listing process for Exchange B, we need a combination of BTC, USDT and EDG to address marketing campaigns and market-maker deposits. 
2. The promotional campaign costs are part of the agreement with Exchange B, and the MM deposits are the means to conform to Exchange B's requirements on liquidity performance. 
3. You can review the docs around these blockers here: [https://edgeware-a.slab.com/posts/exchange-b-blockers-7dyh2dok](https://edgeware-a.slab.com/posts/exchange-b-blockers-7dyh2dok)
4. Additionally, our market-maker has informed me that our reserves of the BTC side of existing market-making is lower than optimal per their trading team- due to a combination of market price of BTC dipping and the trading activity balancing us to be heavier in EDG. They are requesting we deposit 0.6 BTC as soon as possible in order to quote properly. 
5.  Consequently, I would like to include 0.6 BTC worth of EDG in this proposal. Normally I would separate this out into a separate proposal, but_ since the same liquidation plan would be run for the whole set of funds,_ I'm not sure it makes sense to split. 
6. If the community is adamant that this should be a separate proposal I'm happy to organize.



# Proposals and Cost Breakdown

body:
**OVERVIEW**
The [existing](https://beresheet-faucet.vercel.app/) beresheet testnet faucet has been inactive for quite a while now because of which the potential developers are drifting away to other public testnets because of the ease to obtain test tokens. We have developed a new faucet with more functionalities. 

**GOALS**
1. Automatize test token distribution for testing and development on Edgeware.
2. Minimizing entry barriers for new developers by giving them test tokens to play around.
3. This will increase the developer engagement on the network.


**SPECIFICATIONS**
We have added the following new features to the faucet -
- Supports all address encodings as input to send tokens.
- Users can ask for a custom amount with an upper limit to avoid wastage.
- Uses the latest Polkadot API version.
- A banner has been added asking the users to return excess balance after accomplishing their tasks.
- Remaining balance along with the faucet address is being displayed now, so that anyone from the community can refill the faucet to keep it alive.
- Enhanced UI/UX.

Timothée Delabrouille - CEO of Rusty Cewmates - [https://github.com/tdelabro](https://github.com/tdelabro) - [https://www.linkedin.com/in/timotheedelabrouille/](https://www.linkedin.com/in/timotheedelabrouille/) - [https://rustycrewmates.com/](https://rustycrewmates.com/)

## Proposal summary
Update Edgeware Metadata to v.14

## Partner support
We have the support of Rich (Decent Partners) and Ramsey (Decentration), with which we had a few meeting in order to put together our value proposition. They will create the actual on chain proposal, provide the 5% bonding fees and receive a 10% service fee.

## Background information
A few month ago Parity release the `v14` of the Substrate metadata. It introduce the crate `scale-info` and the trait `TypeInfo` that can be implemented on any type making it self descriptive for other programs, making the `#[pallet::metadata` macro obsolete. When using it you don't have to manually declare your custom types in order to interact with the chain API. For those familiar with ethereum-smart contract, it can be seen way for the runtime to self describe its ABI.

## Problem statement
This feature being a really nice improvement to the metadata mechanism, it seems useful to adopt it for Edgeware, which is currently using the v12. The process of migrating to metadata v14 is not complex, but it require to be done consistently in all the pallets of the chain. A basic comprehension of Substrate is required to execute it properly.
This has been requested by @thomivy on github:[ https://github.com/edgeware-network/edgeware-node/issues/4]( https://github.com/edgeware-network/edgeware-node/issues/4)

title: Edgeware DGov: cross-chain governance
body:
# **Edgeware DGov **

This thread is an outline and primer on projects related to Edgeware and DGov. This is not a funding proposal. 

**What is Edgeware DGov?**

[DGov Network ](https://dgov.network)is a nascent chain that aims to develop governance in Web 3.0, founded by Ramsey. **Edgeware DGov** is the projects and proposals toward shared strategic objectives. DGov chain can also be the first out of Edgewares chain factory "incubator/accelerator".

## **Objectives**
There are two main technical objectives for Edgeware DGov currently: a) enabling cross-chain governance and b) enabling layer 2 governance for sub-communities. 

**What will it take for a substrate chain to stake governance into another substrate chain? **

The parity-bridge-common pallet working group has delivered functionality that enables two substrate chains to relay information to each other, without necessarily being connected through a relay network.

This bridging is a more simple version of the relay chain that trades off efficiency and low-cost transactions with a simple way of communicating validated data across chains.

Gavin made a promise that some DOTs could be sent to Kusama. A team was set up to build something that allows for bridging to happen. They did, and [here](https://github.com/paritytech/parity-bridges-common) you can test their pallet and communicate data between two test chains.

**How can we starting experimenting with these new Substrate features?**

This idea enables some interesting use cases. The first interesting - and useful - use case that comes to mind is sharing voting power between chains. 

**What will it take for Edgeware to have a governance stake in the DGov chain?**

Initial aims and objectives:

title: Considering a Cap to Supply + Inflation
body:
As I look at other Polkadot and Substrate chains, I detect that we are the only chain (that the have data on,)  that does not institute a hard cap on supply.

[https://www.parachain.live/](https://www.parachain.live/)

I am wondering whether it would be beneficial for us to set an interim (soft?) cap, obviously subject to future governance action, that will help us  convey more accurately the spirit if not the letter of our disinflationary monetary policy.  

I am especially curious how this intersects with Parachain status: 

- Inflation is used to incentivize network security, something we will pass to DOT as a parachain.
- Inflation also feeds the treasury, but in an ideal setting this is funded purely from a portion of transaction funds, more effectively aligning incentives between treasury growth and network growth. 


An interim cap could be established that effectively targets the date of parachain initiation, so as to not interfere with network security, raise interest in staking today - as there will be a planned cut-off,  and to improve investment thesis on the network.

title: EVM: Updating our Strategy for Frontier
body:
**Summary: **This article discusses the challenges of Frontier, and asks where it fits in Edgeware technical priorities in light of ecosystem and strategic changes since network launch.

-- 

Commonwealth Labs has been working extremely hard on integrating , debugging, and improving our EVM compatibility layer 'Frontier'-  and one of our largest platforms, DTrade, will be leveraging this in a multichain fashion.

When we first began working with Frontier, XDai had just begun to see adoption as a L2 for ETH, and the EVM-specific platform, and within Polkadot, it wasn't yet clear how Moonbeam and other EVM platforms would evolve. 

Today, Polygon and other roll-up platforms have gained not-insignificant share, and we may in a good position to update our priorities.


1. EVM today faces usability issues and eats up a significant portion of our community engineering attention, from my perspective. (Take with a grain of salt, as I may not have the clearest or most up-to-date view.)
2. Dtrade is reliant on EVM working and is one of the larger and more anticipated projects on EDG.
3. ETH Bridges and EVM help facilitate asset transfer to the network, improving some traditional metrics for EDG. 


The existing strategy for EVM is, as I understand it, to enable a 'copy paste' level of deployment ease for teams in ETH who are looking to enter the DOT ecosystem. 

With unfinished research around the parabridge / parachain direction, and the possibility of swappable consensus, I am concerned that encouraging more teams to launch on EVM at this time may be premature - not only because we cannot provide determinative guidance on the direction (bridge/parachain) but because of the current status of EVM.

If we can resolve this functionality soon, and offer at minimum a 1x-- ideally a 10x experience over ETH deployment, I am comfortable continuing with the notion that we can rapidly onboard potentially tens of existing ETH Dapps.

title: On-chain Bounties: Ideas + Meta Discussion
body:
Building a strong community of core developers and tooling/apps developers is important for Edgeware. The root cause of most of our challenges goes back to lack of technical talent on the chain.

Building good on-ramps for technical community members should be a major priority. The bounty system provides a good structure for doing that.

New developers can apply to bounties, which lets them get engaged with the council and community platforms like Discord and Commonwealth. They can jump straight into building something Edgeware needs, rather than trying to come up with their own proposals.

**Kicking off this thread for ideas for bounties**, plus meta-discussion around the bounties system.** **It would be great to have a list of on-chain bounties for the council to fund.

As a matter of procedure, before every bounty goes on chain, it should have its own thread, where it gets discussed for at least a week. The exact phrasing of each bounty should be somewhat carefully considered, and we should ramp up using the bounty system cautiously.

We're targeting that new treasury proposals are not more than $50k, so we should also have a similar cap or rate schedule for treasury bounties (e.g. $5k or $10k). The value of EDG will fluctuate after the bounty is created, so that's just something to keep in mind.

## How the bounty system works

1. **The community agrees to fund a bounty** - for example, this could happen on a weekly community call.
2. **Anyone can propose the bounty**, by putting down a deposit, and specifying a title and amount of EDG.
3. **The council approves the bounty**. This can be done from within Commonwealth or polkadot-js. Approval requires the same number of supporting councillors as a treasury proposal.
4. **The bounty is funded. **At the next spend period, the bounty EDG is taken out of the treasury and reserved.
5. **The council proposes a curator for the bounty.** This also requires an approving council motion.
6. **The curator accepts the bounty.

title: Price, Chain Factories and Positive Sum Worlds
body:
I spent this morning reading the latest post "[Positive Sum Worlds: Remaking Public Goods](https://otherinter.net/research/positive-sum-worlds/)" from [Other Internet ](otherinter.net/)(authors of [Headless Brands)](https://otherinter.net/research/headless-brands/) and other great pieces of research. 

It's a long essay and is essential reading for anyone interested in discussions of what "blockchains are for" and how we can evolve past conversations around price to understand how these amazing new social coordination technologies and the treasuries they enable offer us a path to building a better world over long time horizons. 

> _Can crypto protocols be considered public goods if ownership is concentrated in the hands of a few whales?  Colloquially, these market primitives are sometimes described as "public infrastructure," but if blockchains serve a "public" today, it is primarily one of decentralized finance. _
> _**Fundamentally, these tokenholders share only one common object of concern: price.**_
> _As protocol treasuries transition to community stewardship of public works, it's time to imagine how crypto protocols might uniquely conceive of public goods._

And leading on into the cultural aspects - namely how new ideas are adopted: 

> _French revolutionaries orchestrated a new peoples' self-consciousness by organizing festivals, erecting monuments, and designating new communal spaces (Ozouf, 1975). _
> _In both instances, political bodies were raised to the status of institutions by establishing new venues for storytelling—venues in which people could begin to identify themselves as part of a collective whole, that is, a public._
> _This notion of the public as a self-conscious entity has also taken hold on the internet, where **adoption is driven by publication and circulation of media.** To publish a web document or software application is more than making something public: it's an act of making a public (Warner, 2002)._

title: Proposal: Ecosystem Partner Grant Structure
body:
# Ecosystem Partner Grant 
**Structure Draft**

As part of the Agency's roadmap for this year, we targeted recruiting and supporting 3 'ecosystem partners' on EDG. 


Unlike a standard partner or grant recipient, our approach was to further decentralize the management and development of the EDG ecosystem through strategic and highly capable teams who could drive entire categories of use cases or otherwise serve as anchors for categories like the creator economy, defi, and orgtech. 


This document serves as the starting draft for the grant structure, which would offer very high rewards of EDG - up to percents of the network, in order to forge long term social contracts between the network and development and product teams. 

Note that while our traditional grant structure rewards deliverables and functions, this grant operates on performance metrics related to the growth and adoption of the network. As it is milestone based, teams would only be paid out as a result of reaching goals approved by the community on a per-milestone basis. 

**Link to Google Doc**
[https://docs.google.com/document/d/1R_dwxZ3FtCSMl274M80K4nSzbIAwqCMWtuOHS9DfsZw/edit?usp=sharing](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1R_dwxZ3FtCSMl274M80K4nSzbIAwqCMWtuOHS9DfsZw/edit?usp=sharing) 

## Update July 26

Given the pushback from council members, I don't believe this will go forward for EDG at this time.

This leaves me with one reservation, which is that the Agency proposal is listed to provide three ecosystem partners. If there is to be no ecosystem partner structure, other than our usual grants -- 'traditional partners,' then we will be unable to fulfill and prioritize that item.

Instead, I will pivot instead to recruiting one core team, which I believe is essential to Edgeware's long term success, and treat that process as a one-off to be negotiated with the community ad-hoc.

We will of course continue the traditional grant structure, ongoing business development and launch support.

title: dTrade Update
body:
Hey Edgeware community, after careful assessment and deliberations with all stakeholders, we decided to not deploy dTrade on the Edgeware solo chain. The liquidity providers and market makers working with us require the shared security of the Polkadot relay chain to feel safe about their capital. For that, we have formally partnered with a parachain that will likely be the first live parachain on Polkadot with smart contract and L2 functionality; the results of Kusama auctions and their dev efforts are suggestive of this. We will make a public announcement on this soon. We had a several week testing phase and also involved all of the stakeholders, including our team, our advisors, our investors, the market makers and the liquidity providers. 

We dedicated a considerable effort (several weeks) towards building the Ethereum<>Edgeware bridge and getting it pen tested by a third party auditing firm. As a gesture, we have open-sourced the code, which can be accessed from over here: [https://github.com/dtradeorg/ChainBridge](https://github.com/dtradeorg/ChainBridge). The audit report will be added to the GitHub in a few weeks after the backbox testing phase completes. It likely does not make sense to take it live on Edgeware solo chain but rather on the Edgeware parachain, once it is running. However, that is a decision for the Edgeware developers and community to make. 

We’d like to thank the Edgeware agency and its community members for their support towards dTrade. We look forward to seeing Edgeware progress and grow in the Polkadot ecosystem. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask them on the Edgeware Telegram group, we are happy to remain active there over the next few days.

## Background
Substrate is a bleeding-edge blockchain project. While Edgeware was one of the first chains to adopt and launch, we also faced some of the largest technical hurdles.  Additionally, due to our unique distribution that allocated a supermajority of tokens to community members through the lockdrop, we took risks on a non-standard strategy for maintaining development. 

The downstream effects of this have been to disalign values for powerful investors who could support core teams, as the upside was relatively limited compared to other projects launching over the past several years.  Chains who launched without this feature have had significantly more success in maintaining the development runway.

This matters, because EDG is solely dependent on its own token price for self-development., while other chains are able to deploy both traditional capital and treasury capital.  In a state where liquidity and market price are low, we are hobbled to continue to advance development.

title: Pfeilstorch: A new scene for the Inexact Sciences
body:
_**TL;DR**: Existing knowledge institutions and legitimation pipelines are in crisis. Pfeilstorch is a new, institutionally unaffiliated community for knowledge production, built on a Commonwealth fork and using Edgeware's treasury and governance structure to award microgrants and reputational credit. Our plan is to leverage the chaos of the current moment, and the emergence of new Web3 paradigms, to build cultural technology that supports decentralized research and philosophy. Our focus lies on those topics that existing institutions have shunned due to their messy unreadiness for formal verification and data collecting—topics in the “[inexact sciences](https://twitter.com/literalbanana/status/1247400947472404482?s=21),” such as human communication, social strategy, and representation in the wild._

## Intro

The last decade has seen major changes in research and publishing, as a wave of young thinkers forego traditional institutions for online scenes. And yet old-school forums remain the go-to platform where such writers and researchers can engage in long-form discussion. Substack isolates its writers in semi-paywalled digital newsletters. Twitter, an [“oral” culture](https://twitter.com/ctbeiser/status/1401775079139155970), is too noisy, fragmented, and disorganized for participants to build lasting frameworks together. The Commonwealth forum is a step in the right direction, but currently lacks tools specific to research and publishing. What is needed are discursive platforms which hybridize discussion and publishing, that generate new ideas while keeping cultural memory: a true Web3 knowledge production scene, a system of watering holes for decentralized thinkers. Yet the few present rallying points for “Game B” (i.e. institutionally unaffiliated) thought are [presently](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_dark_web) [consumed](https://twitter.com/peternlimberg/status/1289241648912728065) [by](https://letter.wiki/topics/65)

title: SimpleMajority - a proposed Edgeware governance standard
body:
This is a short post about basic Edgeware governance standards and was prompted by a lively debate ahead of the New-Futures proposal regarding the use of SimpleMajority voting.  

## **What are governance standards?**

We have a blockchain that enshrines the basic rules of Edgeware into on-chain code - how balances, transactions, voting, upgrades and funding amongst others relate to each other and the processes needed to execute certain actions. 

These automated processes work well at the most basic level, however decisions are nuanced, people interpret things in different ways and so we also need some simple off-chain governance standards that allow us define the way the community interprets and uses the basic functionality. 

## **Why do we need governance standards?**

Often standards are already informally agreed, however this leaves room for later disagreement, so we should have a small number of simple but formalised standards that we can return to. 

Having a few basic standards is vital as we move forward as a project - we don't need loads, but these standards should gradually emerge over time as we debate / discuss and iterate.

In essence we take an informal **belief** aka "We believe that proposals should all be decided via a simplemajority vote..."  and formalise this belief into a governance standard. 

## **Proposed Governance standard: SimpleMajority Treasury Proposals**

Currently when anyone puts forward a treasury proposal to a public referendum, the process uses the [SuperMajority standard.](https://wiki.polkadot.network/docs/learn-governance) 

This means that proposals that are put forward can be easily blocked by a small number of people, or even a single individual or group, even if the proposal has broad backing by a large number of smaller community members. 

For the last few proposals, there has been an informal agreement that we put proposals to a SimpleMajority rather than a SuperMajority, meaning they are biased for broad community bac

title: First Steps to Ethereum 2.0: Istanbul Hard Fork Review
body:
## Takeaways

- The Ethereum Istanbul upgrade, originally meant to be implemented in October, is now hopefully scheduled for December 4th.
- With the hard fork, Ethereum’s Proof of Work process will change to the controversial ProgPoW, the virtual machine will be upgraded to Web Assembly Code, and account versioning will be implemented.
- Istanbul is the first of Ethereum’s planned upgrades on its journey to becoming Ethereum 2.0: a Proof-of-Stake platform with database sharding for increased scalability.
- Questions about Istanbul and the potential lack of a viable exit mechanism from Ethereum have led many to ask: Will Ethereum 2.0 be a solution, or bring more problems?

### What’s at Stake with the Istanbul Fork?

The Istanbul hard fork is the first of Ethereum’s planned upgrades on its journey to becoming Ethereum 2.0: a Proof-of-Stake platform with database sharding for increased scalability. The Istanbul hard fork, which was originally meant to be implemented in October but is now hopefully scheduled for December 4th, integrates six Ethereum Improvement Proposals (EIPs) (Paradigm). This is all just the beginning of the lead up to Ethereum 2.0, which is meant to be activated with the Serenity upgrade at some point in the next few years. 

Perhaps the most controversial element of Istanbul is the new mining algorithm, which will change Ethereum’s Proof of Work process to something called ProgPoW. According to a researcher from Nuo Network, the change to ProgPoW was approved by 100% of miners and 94% of token holders (Seth). However, it’s seen strong push-back in the community, because the change in mining algorithm will disadvantage ASIC miners. 

The Ethereum virtual machine, which facilitates the execution of smart contracts and subsequently the running of dApps, will be upgraded to Web Assembly Code and account versioning will be implemented to allow for breaking features to be applied while maintaining smooth execution of other smart contracts (eth.wiki).

title: The Promise of On-Chain Governance for Cooperation: Blockchain and Co-ops
body:
## Takeaways

- The International Co-operative Alliance defines a co-operative as "**an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social, and cultural needs and aspirations** through a jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise." 
- Co-operative organizations have higher productivity levels, employee wages, and profits. **They incorporate all the ideals necessary for sustainable development, but they often lack the starting capital and appropriate governance models that can help them survive long-term.**
- **Co-ops could benefit hugely from the use of blockchain-based community organizing.** There is a culture match between the principles behind blockchain technology and the ideals of cooperativism, as well as a parallel between the opportunity for evolution necessitated by the co-operative model and [that provided by on-chain governance mechanisms](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/140-organizational-governance-mechanisms-for-blockchains). 

### What’s a co-op and where did they come from?

The International Co-operative Alliance (ICA) defines a co-operative as "an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social, and cultural needs and aspirations through a jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise." The idea of a co-op is ancient, but these organizations started to become formally structured and implemented throughout the 18th century, as increased urbanization meant people struggled to obtain basic food needs. When textile mill workers from Rochdale, England went on strike in 1843 and the strike failed, 28 people founded the Rochdale Equitable Pioneers Society to open a food store as an alternative to the company store. This was not the first official co-op, but it was the first to be successful long-term (Co+op).

title: Concerns About New Dai
body:
MakerDAO’s [transition to Multi-Collateral Dai (MCD)](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/126-potential-lessons-from-multicollateral-dai) is accompanied by the establishment of “Synthetic Assets,” a Dai Savings Rate smart contract, and a potential new governance model that uses oracles and algorithms to manage the stability fee keeping Dai pegged to the dollar. These all sound exciting, and the MakerDAO team hopes the transition to MCD will open the space to a much broader user base. But it’s left many of us wondering: **will the new Dai fix any of the problems that Sai already had? What new challenges will arise?**  

A 2017 code review of MakerDAO’s Sai revealed opportunities for participants to game the system, including a way for whales to capture rewards meant for PETH holders (Baylina et al.). This was not the only serious issue the team of code reviewers found, and as they concluded: “We believe there are likely to be more issues in this code beyond what have been identified, and addressing the issues described in this document may introduce more bugs into the system.” 

While the MakerDAO team did offer a blog post responding to the major issues found, there are still questions about what new problems MCD may bring. This is important, because as MakerDAO has recently explained, “MCD is essentially a decentralized system without any operator. Once deployed onto the blockchain, it operates in an autonomous way.” In other words, it’s crucial that the team thinks through issues in the design of the system, given its autonomous execution.

The potential to use “real-world” collateral to back MCD has also triggered anxiety in the MakerDAO community. title: Designing DAO Primitives: The Exit Mechanism
body:
## Takeaways

- Effective exit mechanisms are a crucial aspect of an optimal governance system. **The possibility of exit can both incentivize a group to collaborate successfully and allow for the organic formation of like-minded communities.** 
- If exit is too easy, then a community could face a lack of a strong, long-term participant base. This could lead to network actions that are, like the community,  fleetingly useful and lacking sustainability. Therefore, an exit mechanism could be intentionally designed to force slower group evolution. 
- While it may be beneficial to design exit mechanisms that support lasting participation, it’s also important to be able to leave a group that you don’t agree with. **What types of DAO exit mechanisms could we experiment with to target both of these goals?** 

## Exit Strategies for DAOs

An intentionally-built exit mechanism is an important DAO primitive, but it's another aspect of DAO governance that we haven’t yet seen enough experimentation with to develop industry best practices. To some degree, **the possibility of exit can incentivize the entire group to collaborate more efficiently and selflessly,** working toward group utility to keep the group together. At the same time, **the ability to leave freely and flow between groups allows for the organic formation of like-minded communities.**

An open-source DAO makes it technically possible for anybody to leave, at any time, because they can just copy and paste the code from the original DAO and start their own version (Grx). However, this could lead to a situation in which a small group of divisive stakeholders with loud voices drive away other organization participants who feel like their perspective is not well-represented or supported in the group (even though it very well may be). While these other organization participants could theoretically exit and start their own version of the DAO, they may not have the network or reputation to see the same amount of particip

title: How Should a DAO Be Defined?
body:
Decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) are exploding right now. We’re starting to see them take very unique shapes - from DAOs wrapped as legally compliant LLCs, to DAOs that hope to replace nation-states. This explosion has given us a lot of different concepts and terminology around DAOs, which begs the question: What really is the definition of a DAO? **What are some other words we could use for DAO?** 

This question gets a bit complicated thinking about the differences between types of decentralized organizations. For instance, in [a terminology guide](https://blog.ethereum.org/2014/05/06/daos-dacs-das-and-more-an-incomplete-terminology-guide/) by Vitalik Buterin, a Decentralized Autonomous Corporation/Company (DAC) is defined by the fact that “there is a concept of shares in a DAC which are purchaseable and tradeable in some fashion, and those shares potentially entitle their holders to continual receipts based on the DAC’s success.” So there should be a nominal distinction between a DAO that has a standard shareholder framework and offers financial returns on investments, and a DAO that doesn’t. 

Buterin also distinguishes between DAOs and DC’s: Decentralized Communities. This one is straightforward - there are not smart contracts defining any collective action by a DC, as there are in a DAO. However, the distinction drawn between a DAO and a DO (decentralized organization) is not so clear.  In Buterin's words, this is because “there is really no difference between a certain set of actors making decisions directly and that set of actors controlling all of the information through which decisions are made.” That is to say, even if the decentralized org is not technically autonomous, if a small group is controlling the people’s understanding of governance options, then the actions of the group could be as limited or defined as if some group was writing smart contracts to execute them.

title: Identity for a multi-chain ecosystem
body:
For most blockchain applications besides wallets, there is a single blockchain that runs that application. Be it Aragon on Ethereum or Counterparty on Bitcoin, many protocols and dApps are mono-chain apps. They rely on the underlying public key system as the identity system. The key question we ask: is there a better way to handle identities?

This question presents a new set of user experience challenges. In a multi-chain world, will users even want to maintain multiple private key pairs when they are using an arbitrary web dApplication? I will address this question negatively first, as I believe this is not how users will want to interface with blockchain applications. Instead, the point of the user experience will exist on a spectrum that highlights the difference between the Web2 world and the Web3 world.

Web2 vs. Web3 Authentication
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
As a motivating example, take Facebook and Google login: a single sign-on service for most applications one uses on the internet today, which only requires access to one username/password pair. This construction allows the user no privacy, but it allows them complete convenience. The user never has to maintain private keys, not even a single keypair, because in the event of losing one's password, you can redeem it using password recovery methods.

Now consider the growing multi-chain blockchain landscape: different key signing algorithms for each new or existing blockchain in which one holds cryptocurrencies. A plethora of applications, specific to each chain, that requires secure storage of one's private keys so that funds are never lost or stolen. In some ways this mimics a world akin to password management and as the list of blockchains grows, one is left with similar problems of remembering (storing) passwords in a safe location. Nonetheless, there is money involved and one is never instructed to store private keys on hosted password manageme

title: What Does an Ideal Token Distribution Look Like?
body:
## Takeaways

- If you want to assess an ideal token distribution, first you need to decide what the goals of token distribution are.
- The most common idea behind an ideal token distribution is the maximization of decentralization.
- The opportunity to implement mechanisms of game theory and crypto-economics means that goals for token distribution could potentially go beyond simply having a low Gini coefficient.

### What does the ideal token distribution look like?

Token distribution is a key element to the success of a blockchain network. Concerns about [vote-buying for EOS](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/90-eos-votebuying-and-power-distribution) and potential [validator centralization in the Cosmos network](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/118-diversifying-delegations-stake-distribution-the-cosmos-example) show the importance of token distribution for protocol governance, security, and sustainability. But what does the ideal token distribution actually look like? 

The question breaks down to a few parts. **What are the goals of token distribution? How do we implement them, and how can we measure the results?**

A foundational principle behind ideal token distribution is maximal decentralization. The most common way to measure decentralization in token distribution is with a Gini coefficient calculation. For some context, Ethereum’s Gini coefficient is 0.798, and Bitcoin Cash is 0.754 (Parsiq). These aren’t necessarily bad, but we’ve set a new standard with the Edgeware lockdrop: recent [analysis of Edgeware’s token distribution gave a Gini-coefficient of 0.694](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/102-examining-the-edgeware-lockdrop-gini-coefficients-and-successes).

title: What Are the Benefits of a Crypto Debit Card?
body:
I’m curious - does anybody use crypto credit or debit cards? I don’t use one myself, so I’m wondering if people think they're actually secure, or why people use their particular crypto debit card. 

There seem to be a few debit cards available for Bitcoin and Ethereum, which you can use at any store. These cards are backed by credit providers that everyone recognizes: Visa and Mastercard. It would be huge for adoption if these trusted providers continue to support everyday use of cryptos - but in 2018, Visa started backing out of its relationships with many major crypto-card providers, including BitPay and WaveCrest (Irby). According to one report, as of last week there were only four major companies supplying crypto debit cards: Wirex, Coinbase, Bitpay, and Cryptopay (Beigel). 

Common coins supported besides BTC and ETH include Ripple (XRP) and Litecoin (LTC). Challenges seem to include high processing fees, dealing with exchange rates, and jurisdiction limitations. These are all in addition to major credit providers increasingly dropping support for crypto-debit cards. Anybody know why this shift is happening? 

Crypto credit cards, on the other hand, don’t really exist yet - though some are innovating in that space. For instance, Nexo is offering an insured, crypto-backed credit line to twenty-three cryptocurrencies, and claims to be the only crypto bank account that lets you borrow in more than forty-five fiat currencies. 

In the context of major credit providers backing out of relationships with crypto debit card suppliers, does it make sense to get a crypto debit card? Are there more benefits to using a crypto credit card like what Nexo is offering? Does it make sense to have a crypto card at all?

title: Foundational Text: The Governance of Blockchain Dispute Resolution
body:
“The question, then, is whether the dispute resolution problem can be more effectively solved through blockchain-based mechanisms.” Researchers Darcy W. E. Allen, Aaron Lane, and Marta Poblet from RMIT University explore some pioneering smart contract solution methods in their recently published paper [“The Governance of Blockchain Dispute Resolution”](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3334674). Smart contracts have created new types of disputes, usually related to their automatic execution and human error in design. These novel conflicts require re-designed resolution mechanisms. At the same time, the RMIT researchers make the compelling case that smart contracts could also serve as alternative dispute resolution tools for challenges outside of the crypto ecosystem. 

The paper offers both a framework for blockchain-based institutional dispute resolution primitives, which they term the Dispute Resolution Possibility Frontier (DRPF), as well as case studies of current blockchain-based solution mechanisms. One case study looks at Jury.Online, which offers a dispute resolution process that relies on the random selection of autonomous, anonymous jurors and judges from an expert pool. Kleros presents a similar system with its Crowdsourced Online Dispute Resolution (CODR) mechanism. 

Another case looks at the dispute avoidance system of Mattereum, which puts assets in control of an automated “custodian” to ensure contract execution and relies on a technically knowledgeable mediator should further issues arise. The researchers also describe the LTO platform’s Ricardian live contract, which differs from a smart contract in that the contract itself does not autonomously execute, but instead prepares the infrastructure for execution and allows for off-chain changes.

While the Commonwealth team has encouraged the formation of this sort of group for a long time, we think an ambassador program can be more than volunteers spreading the word. title: What Types of Legally Compliant DAOs Are There?
body:
## Takeaways

- In the US, for a DAO to be legally compliant it needs to be wrapped as a legally registered business. So far, this has looked like DAOs working with individual states to register as LLCs.
- OpenLaw is working to offer a library of other potential legal wrappers and automatic filing services to facilitate more straightforward onboarding to legal compliance 
- There are still many nuanced questions about what it means to be a legal DAO, especially regarding privacy laws and regulations in other parts of the world. 

### What are some legal DAOs?

In the US, for a DAO to be legally compliant it needs to be wrapped as a legally registered business. dOrg, which claims it was the first legally compliant DAO in the US, was formed based on Vermont’s Blockchain-Based Limited Liability Company (BBLLC) law. The BBLLC law makes it possible to “reference blockchain code (smart contracts in our case) as the legitimate source of authority for their company’s operations and governance” (Biggs). 

Meanwhile, Blockstack claims to have offered the first SEC-approved ICO in the history of the US, which opened on July 11th of this year. With the SEC’s Regulation A+ framework, the sale was open to both accredited and non-accredited investors. Blockstack Token, which facilitated the token sale and blockchain, is an LLC (Ali). 

OpenLaw followed a similar track, originally working with Aragon and New York State to set further precedence for a DAO wrapped in an LLC. They’ve recently turned that effort into a framework for “resurrecting The DAO,” in the form of a Limited Liability Autonomous Organization: The LAO. To comply with the SEC’s stance on ICOs, only accredited investors will be able to put stake in the OpenLaw LAO, as the coins spent to buy into the LAO will be viewed as security tokens (Byrne). OpenLaw is also offering a library of other potential legal wrappers and automatic filing services to facilitate more straightforward onboarding to legal compliance for DAOs

title: Validator Campaign: stake.fish
body:
Hello everyone! I wanted to share stake.fish's validator campaign with the Edgeware community.

**1. What is your experience as a validator or node operator? What other protocols are you validating on right now, if any?**

Our founder, Wang Chun, has co-founded f2pool, one of the largest Bitcoin and Ethereum mining pools in 2013. He has been running and maintaining nodes on various Proof of Work chains for the mining pool. Our head of infrastructure, Kris Lucera, has 18 years of experience working on systems architecture and infrastructure security. He has been bringing cybersecurity best practices to the blockchain world.

stake.fish has been in operations for over a year. During that time we have run validators or nodes on: EOS mainnet, Cosmos Hub, Tezos, Chainlink, Algorand, The OAN (Aion), Kusama, Storj, Loom Network, IRIS Network, BOS, and Lino Network. We also have nodes on various testnets: Solana, NEAR Protocol, NuCypher, Oasis Labs, and Elrond.

**2. What's your technical setup?**

We make strategic use of both on-premise and cloud infrastructure. We try not to disclose too much on our infrastructure setup for security reasons. When asked about our capabilities, we like to point to our track record of running infrastructure on different networks for the past year without any issues. We will bring the same level of expertise to our Edgeware validator.

**3. How did you learn about Edgeware? Why are you interested in validating?**

While there are many (many) items on our checklist while conducting due diligence on projects, they can eventually be summarized in two questions. One, is the project working on something interesting? Two, is the community interested in building and staking on top of the project? To both these questions, Edgeware was a strong yes, and so therefore we want to support it as soon as possible.

**4. What are your positions on issues that governance will be expected to handle?**

We will have to review governance proposals case-by-case.

title: Edgeware Community Standards
body:
Agreeing on community conduct standards is key for supporting strong collective action. Below is a proposal for Edgeware Community Guidelines. Let’s talk and make a version we can get some consensus on!

1. Be exceptionally kind.
2. Be respectful - but we should flesh out what this means.  
3. Freedom of speech is expected (but see rules #1 and 2). 
4. No illegal activity.
5. No harassment of any sort. 
6. No spam. Only contribute discussion and votes that you, as an individual, genuinely think offer value and are to the benefit of the community. 
7. If you’re offering criticism, be constructive.
8. Share the space, be inclusive. Try to be empathetic and allow everybody to get their voice in.  

I think it’s good to keep it fairly simple and focus on the principles behind the code of conduct rather than setting very strict rules. Do you agree? 

One place where this might not apply would be if the community decides we should have a clear dispute resolution system set in place. But perhaps that should be part of a different discussion. Would anybody be interested in working together to craft a mediation process proposal for Edgeware?

title: How Blockchains Could Change the Tax System: Harberger and DAOs
body:
The implementation of a Harberger Tax in a DAO is a crazy experiment - one that could show us new ways to think about the value of money, assets, and human engagement. 

**A Harberger Tax is a standard tax percentage that applies to assets with self-assessed values.** It’s a concept that’s been made popular recently by Glen Weyl and Eric Posner, in their book *Radical Markets.* It’s also one of the founding principles behind RadicalxChange, a group started by Weyl and Vitalik Buterin. In that space, it is called the “Common Ownership Self-Assessed Tax (COST)” (Tang & Peng).

The idea is that the owner of an asset chooses its value, meaning they know how much will be collected in taxes on that asset. However, they have to balance the incentive to value their assets at a low price with the fact that, in the Harberger Tax system, anyone can buy an asset at any time if they pay the price the owner valued it at. The balance should allow assets to shift towards the people who genuinely value them and will use them in the most worthwhile ways, resulting in fewer monopolies across more democratic markets.  

**The system is designed in hopes of getting at the true value of an asset**, as defined by constructive use or otherwise meaningful engagement. NFT marketplaces like Decentraland, OpenSea, and Harberger Ads are already using the Harberger Tax system to run liquid markets for digital goods (Riady). If an Edgeware group wanted to spin up a DAO to facilitate any sort of Harberger marketplace, taxes could go to the DAO treasury, with the choice on how to use it left to the community.

The Harberger Tax system has also been suggested for DAO leadership. A council member could put a value on their leadership position, and anyone who can match that value will be able to take their spot (Heynes). In this case, the taxes could be collected daily for as long as the counselor was in a leadership position. The taxes could either be returned to the council member after they are dep

title: How To: Valuing Cryptocurrencies
body:
## Takeaways

- Evolving blockchain-based marketplaces offer a chance to escape the problems of centralized financial systems and create novel DeFi techniques - including new valuation models for cryptocurrencies
- Traditional models for valuing assets could potentially be effective for legally compliant, for-profit DAOs. But other models are needed for DAOs with different goals and cryptos that are not meant to be used in the same way traditional assets are. 
- While several models have been introduced in recent years, there is still a need for crypto-valuation models that weigh the utility, scarcity, and perceived value of coins with diverse functions.

### What are some valuation models for cryptocurrencies?

The advent of blockchain tech has led to unique markets for cryptocurrencies, crypto-games, digital collectibles, and [curation schemes](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/142-tests-and-opportunities-for-curation-markets), among others. **These evolving marketplaces offer a chance to escape the problems of centralized financial systems and require the creation of novel DeFi techniques - including new valuation models for cryptocurrencies.** 

Traditional models for valuing assets include a Price/Earnings ratio, a Discounted Cash Flow, and the Gordon Growth Model (Liquid). Given that these models are designed for companies with stock and cash flow, they probably would only be applicable in a for-profit DAO - which may be a type of organization we see more and more of with efforts to offer [legal frameworks for compliant DAOs](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/155-what-types-of-legally-compliant-daos-are-there). 

**But what about organizations that are not for-profit? Or cryptos that are not meant to be used as a security or in this traditional way, but instead as a utility token?** 

ARK Investments, one of the first groups to formally value cryptocurrencies, used a model describes by the equation MV = PQ, where M = Size

A big part of this question can be answered by asking, how do people learn to be blockchain developers? Many in the field now are autodidacts and have benefited hugely from community support. title: Token Distribution Experiments for Network Health
body:
As we consider [the ultimate goals of token distribution](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/151-what-does-an-ideal-token-distribution-look-like), we might also think about what types of distribution mechanisms we can experiment with as we strive to reach those goals. To intentionally design some token distribution experiments, we might first look at wealth redistribution efforts by traditional governments, data on token use in Ethereum, diversely shaped token bonding curves, and the potential integrations of a community engagement reward mechanism. 

Some initial questions:

- Are there inevitable distribution states of major currencies/tokens? What might they be, and are they desirable?
- Does designing different origination structures result in stable or metastable long-term distribution results?
- If this isn’t a problem that can be managed from the bottom-up, can we manage it with a top-level mechanism?

## Outcomes of Original Distribution States

*Wealth Redistribution in Real-World Governments*

For our first example to ask whether or not major currencies have an inevitable distribution state, let’s take a look at one of the most graspable examples we have: modern country economies. Researchers from MIT have shown that economies that start with a more equal income distribution will see less wealth redistribution efforts. Wealth redistribution efforts can be seen as a way to combat centralization, a reaction to too much money pooling in too few hands. Because its initial wage distribution is more equally distributed compared to most capitalist economies, Japan’s government does not do much work to change wealth distribution. Socialist planned economies are largely the same: the government does not need to engage in wealth redistribution efforts because the people *don’t* have any capital and land income, and *do* have set wage rates (Rossner & Barkley).

- How can we best shift ownership of communication channels to the community? Should Councillors play a key role in managing these channels, or perhaps a new “Admin” position?
- Are there content curation mechanisms the community wants to play with - like a curation market, or a TCR? 

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As we think about the future of Edgeware, decentralizing all governance processes is weighing heavy on everybody’s mind. The sharing of information is one of those key processes. How can we plan to transfer the ownership of Edgeware media channels from Commonweath Labs to the community?

These channels include the HeyEdgeware Twitter account, the Discord space, the Telegram group, and the subReddit. In terms of establishing admins for the social media accounts, that could be as simple as nominations and then a community vote on who should serve as admins. This could also be a decision we leave up to Council members. Hand-in-hand with this issue is the question of whether these channels could be better integrated into the Commonwealth.im governance platform. 

But what about the actual sharing of content? Right now, Commonwealth Labs primarily shares content with these channels in hopes of providing useful information to the community. What if there was a way for our community to collectively decide what content gets posted to our social media channels?

title: Inflation is Problematic. How Can We Stop Arbitrary Inflation of EDG?
body:
**It is a source of uncertainty for exchanges and coin holders that the supply of EDG could be inflated arbitrarily using on-chain governance.** It is in all EDG holder’s best interest to agree to prevent that. How can we design a proposal to limit arbitrary inflation? 

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dillon Chen has suggested a proposal that seeks agreement among all yes-voters to pledge to:
- Never increase annual on-chain inflation to higher than 20% per year.
- Never conduct an irregular state transition that causes a discontinuous increase of on-chain supply. (This does not apply to funds that were locked).
- To vote against any instances of the above.

20% is the current inflation rate. As this is what we’re starting with, it feels like this should be the maximum inflation - but of course, community input on this is welcome. We can also consider the goal elucidated in [the Edgeware whitepaper](https://arena-attachments.s3.amazonaws.com/3850782/1928e31873075de95992d4987eb14a2e.pdf?1552432633): “tie inflation to a specific participation or security rate, with the inflation floating up or down to reach a desired total stake.”

We should seriously consider the amount of inflation we allow, and we should take this as a way to bake a rejection of arbitrary inflation right into our community culture. While it might look like an unenforceable social contract, the evidence supporting the disadvantages of inflation is stacked in a way that I believe we, as a network, could collectively and sustainably agree to uphold it. 

A good recent example: Stellar Protocol recently burned *half* of its token supply and eliminated inflation. Their roadmap had a few pieces. First, they had to integrate the plugin into a sidebar with a control panel. title: Foundational Text: A Cypherpunk's Manifesto
body:
“Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.” So begins “[A Cypherpunk’s Manifesto](https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html),” written by Eric Hughes in 1993. The manifesto set off a movement that began percolating following works by early cryptographers like David Chaum: a movement to give the people control over their own identities and actions. The Cypherpunks gave us some of the foundational principles behind cryptocurrency, and their spirit has pushed us to think of even more global use cases for blockchain technology, from reinventing democracy to decentralizing the internet. 

Hughes’ manifesto points to the importance of building anonymous transaction systems, building code that protects the people, and a collaborative effort to realize the future of self-sovereignty that the Cypherpunks imagined. Since its publication, we’ve seen a virtual Cambrian explosion in cryptographic technology. As we continue down this rabbit hole, it feels significant that the words of one of the original fighters for blockchain-based freedom still ring true in many contexts: 

“We cannot expect governments, corporations, or other large, faceless organizations to grant us privacy out of their beneficence...we must defend our own privacy if we expect to have any.”

title: The State of Holographic Consensus
body:
**Takeaways**
- Holographic consensus is an innovative governance idea that uses prediction markets to sort through proposals for an organization, highlighting those that are most likely to pass in a global vote. 
- The need to sort proposals is a result of the limited attention and voting ability inherent to any organization that sees a large number of proposals.
- This governance mechanism is designed to facilitate organization scaling. However, an important question might be whether or not the prediction markets can accurately keep up with large-scale growth in amount of proposals. 


**What is holographic consensus?**

Holographic consensus, introduced originally by Matan Field of DAOstack, is an innovative governance idea that applies prediction markets to the issue of voting. Each proposal in an organization has a prediction market that indicates the likelihood that the proposal will pass in a community-wide vote. This mechanism is used to highlight proposals that the prediction markets indicate are most relevant to the community, which are moved to a “boosted queue” (Field).

The need to sort proposals is a result of the limited attention and voting ability inherent to any organization that sees a large number of proposals. If a DAO has 1,000 active proposals, for instance, there is no way that the entire community will be able to view and vote on each one. Thus, the name holographic consensus speaks to the fact that an ideal governance system would allow for a small amount of voting power to result in alignment with the global opinion of the organization. This makes a hologram, in which each pixel actually contains information for the entire picture, a good metaphor for the governance structure (Field). 

**Application**

Holographic consensus has been tested on DAOstack’s Genesis Protocol. Aragon has also built [a test implementation](https://blog.aragon.one/my-first-aragon-app-voting-supercharged-with-daostacks-holographic-consensus-part-4/) for a holograp

title: Introducing a Decentralized Currency Name Service
body:
## Takeaways

- When currencies are created or old currencies change their names, there are challenges to helping user communities navigate the nomenclature shifts. In the crypto community, there is even more chance for confusion given both how abundant and how similar currency names and abbreviations are.
- A solution to these challenges, as well as the issue of the limited namespace for currencies, could be to set up a Currency Name Service: a DNS-like system for currency name registration (but decentralized).
- Are there challenges to creating this Currency Name Service? How can we best set up a network for decentrally securing the registry? What sort of registration bid process would best fit a Currency Name Service?


------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In 1993, Mexico changed the name of the peso to the “nuevo peso.” They minted new notes, and the value of 1000 pesos became one nuevo peso. They started out by denoting the new currency with an “N” before the word peso, but in 1996 they dropped the N and simply used the original “peso” - even though the meaning behind the name had a very different value. Today, the peso is still technically the nuevo peso. The currency abbreviation, which before 1993 was MXP, is today MXN: the Mexican Nuevo Peso. 

So what did everybody do with their old peso notes after 1993? At what point did people stop using their old peso notes, and transition to the nuevo peso? When did people start using peso to refer to nuevo peso, instead of the original currency? When did the original currency lose its value?

These are questions that are relevant today in the case of MakerDAO’s recent [transition to Multi-Collateral Dai](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/126-potential-lessons-from-multicollateral-dai). title: Managing a Public Fund: The Aragon 1,000 DAI Payout Controversy
body:
“I owe $650 for SEO service for selling my books and some money to my parents for a share in the house and the food.” 

[Quote](https://forum.aragon.org/t/is-it-realistic-to-get-1000-dai-from-agp10-every-month/1519) the Aragon community member who requested 1,470 DAI from the AGP-10 Community Funding DAO - after they were awarded the money. They did not include what the money would be used for in their request proposal, yet the proposal passed - with a single vote. They went on to ask whether or not they could rely on the Community Funding DAO for 1,000 DAI every month. 

The Aragon community funding DAO is meant to encourage and support contribution to the Aragon community and projects - not ambiguous UBI payouts to individuals. While the community fund proposal template is not required, it is still highly recommended to avoid situations like this one.  

Responses from the Aragon community and leadership fell along a spectrum of confusion to hostility. The fact that the awarded DAI did not go towards bettering the Aragon ecosystem was cited as an abuse of the public fund and a clear reason for why the money should be returned (which it eventually was, at the consistent suggestion of Aragon leadership).  

While the core team did resolve the situation, this may be an indication that a public fund needs a formalized funding request process, perhaps including a minimum quorum for votes on funding proposals.

title: Validating on Mainnet
body:
When we soft-launched on September 15th, validators who had submitted a campaign proposal and validated on testnets over the summer were invited to join the genesis validator set.
Once the chain turned on, we noticed many validators were slashed due to incorrectly configured keys. This accounted for the great majority of slashing events at the time, more than any technical issues with Substrate. It also caused the chain to stall unnecessarily.
As a result, we’re now planning to launch mainnet with a much smaller validator set of only Commonwealth nodes. We think this will allow the upcoming network launch proceed much more smoothly, reducing uncertainty and allowing everyone to have a better experience.

title: The Legality of Prediction Markets
body:
## **Takeaways**

- Prediction markets let participants bet on whether or not they think a proposed outcome will come true. The odds are crowdsourced, and the results are shockingly accurate. 
- While prediction markets can be used for illegal gambling, the foundational idea of a prediction market is not illegal. However, prediction markets can get into tricky territory with the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission if they include exchanges offering binary trades. Some markets, like PredictIt, get around this issue with a no-action letter.
- While freedom of speech laws in the US might also apply to the code of prediction markets, they could still face legality issues when it comes to illegal hedging or assassination markets. 
- Prediction markets have come up in proposals for how to build on Edgeware, and they’re particularly important if we want to implement [holographic consensus](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/173-the-state-of-holographic-consensus). Which of these legality issues might apply across applications? Are there other legal challenges for prediction market use cases not discussed here?


-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**How Do Prediction Markets Work?**

Prediction markets have been an academic subject for decades. They’ve long been used in the corporate world, and have seen popularity in the crypto ecosystem with platforms like Augur or governance mechanisms like holographic consensus. In prediction markets like those on Augur, you can bet on anything – even something as mundane or fluid as the weather. These markets let participants bet on whether or not they think a proposed outcome will come true.

title: Edgeware: Day One
body:
Two big announcements:

- We are planning for Edgeware 1.0 mainnet to launch on February 12, 2020.
- We'll also release a major update to Commonwealth at that time — including new functionality around governance, funding, and community organization.


From the beginning, Edgeware has been about building a [crypto network with better governance](https://medium.com/commonwealth-labs/meet-edgeware-25e881e4a37e), and we've always believed that open governance can make a blockchain successful. By our definition, that means building a system that allows all kinds of stakeholders to participate, whether they're large or small, technical or non-technical.
Doing this well will let us build a new kind of decentralized network, which has a much larger audience of developers and users. We think this change will be transformative, the same way Git and Github were transformative for the world of open source.

To illustrate, here are a few goals we want to achieve:
### One system to capture, discuss, and fund new projects & improvements
Blockchain projects have been experimenting with community-funded treasury systems for many years (Decred and Dash were some of the first). But we think such a system needs to be as friendly and rich as a social network to reach its full potential.
Here's how we imagine it working:

- A project might begin its life as a single tweet, which gets saved in a thread for further discussion. Different stakeholders can contribute to the thread by asking questions or providing feedback; this process will identify potential points of collaboration, and help work through tradeoffs.
- As the discussion matures, councillors and stakeholders can signal their support for funding the idea through a treasury proposal, which can then be voted upon and disbursed within the UI.
- While this happens, we'll let developers build their profiles, establish their areas of expertise, and indicate their level of interest in different projects. Sometimes, this will involve de

title: Staking Facilities Validator Campaign
body:
### 
**1. What is your experience as a validator or node operator?**

We started our journey at Staking Facilities in 2017 when we witnessed the emergence of numerous Proof-of-Stake protocols and a lack of professional validators to operate those networks. With the launch of the Tezos network almost two years ago, we opened our services to the public. Ever since our goal was to make staking as easy and accessible as possible for everyone. Over the past year we added other PoS blockchains to our services and built products such as a multi-asset staking-dashboard and an in-browser delegation tool in order to improve the staking experience. In addition, we engage in community work by hosting meetups and creating educational content. We do so in order to make the onboarding as smooth as possible and grow the overall staking economy. We were able to stand our ground and stress-test our set-up successfully under real-market conditions during Cosmos' Game of Stakes. Staking Facilities is self-financed and self-sustaining in order to provide independent, holistic staking services. Additionally, for every project, we have a substantial amount of "skin in the game" as to best align our interests with those of our customers.

**2. What's your technical setup? (cloud vs. on-premise; software stack; key management)**

Most of our infrastructure is running on our own bare metal hardware which is spread out across multiple private racks in top-notch datacenters. We also make use could services to improve peering and latencies, but also to shield our validators from the public internet. Whenever possible our validators make use of enterprise-grade HSMs, such as the YubiHSM, to sign blocks. Additionally, our advanced monitoring system detects network anomalies quickly, allowing us to respond to incidents immediately.

title: Speckle Browser Native Support for Edgeware
body:
Speckle is a multi-chain browser extension for the Polkadot ecosystem, and we want to provide native and ongoing support for Edgeware within the app.

We are currently building support for the Polkadot Relay Chain, and we want to provide cross-compatible support for Edgeware. We are testing integration with the Edgeware testnet at the moment, but we our goal is to provide ongoing and updated support.

While the user will be able to add any substrate network to the extension, native support for Edgeware will enable us to also provide functionality and features that may be specific to the Edgeware chain itself. Further, we are creating a parachain and dapp discovery system, so the user will be able to discover, filter and select chains that they want to interact with upon account creation. This is a great step towards increasing user awareness and adoption.

We also aim to make the extension usable with the Commonwealth governance interface, so accounts created on Speckle can be used to create Web 3 identities. We want to make Speckle one of the premium ways to access Edgeware.

title: DAOs: A Reference Model
body:
DAOs (Decentralized autonomous organizations) have been written about extensively. [1] In short, they are blockchain-based organization conducted through distributed governance. While the form is still evolving, Edgeware can be an ideal place to experiment. As a start, we'd like to recreate existing experiments that seem to have gone well:

- Share-based MolochDAO / MetaCartel style DAOs
- Advanced bonding curve DAOs (such as is built by Commonstack.)

Once those primitives have been built, we can move on to building ones with different voting mechanisms. It would be interesting to see this be funded by the treasury. Based on the discussion here, We'll try to create some signals and treasury proposals to fund development.

Hopefully, DAOs have several other properties:

- Scalability: Whether DAOs are composed of three members or 3 million members, decision making should scale up or down—(from 10 EDG to 10 billion EDG!)
- Resiliency: The ability for a DAO to achieve relevant, accurate and time-sensitive, perhaps even speedy, representation of the participant's interests.
- Transparency: Raw, unfiltered, and accessible information about the total of actions and positions of the DAO.

It remains to be seen how well these experiments are able to meet other criteria for DAOs. There have already been examples of vote buying[2] and slow decision-making show that DAOs still do not have all the desired traits above.

They have several common features:

- Some unit of account of voting power, or even several. These may include shareholder-style governance, or measures of reputation (sometimes characterized as an aggregate of recent contribution, which decays over time.)

- Identity, which is often pseudonymous or anonymous.

- A Legislative process, that is, proposal-making systems.

- An open or closed but authenticating process for individuals to become participating members. This may be as easy as acquiring a governance token, or making a forum account, or showing up to a

title: Creating the EDG Mainnet validation set
body:
We're gearing up to have a distributed launch. While it's great for decentralization, it can be a little tough for coordination, especially given the open participation of the lockdrop. With that said, there are a few preliminary rules we want to set to be included as a validator in the initial genesis spec.

At launch, we plan on having 25-50 nodes in the active set; To be in the set, validators should perform a few actions:

- should have validated in the testnet for at least 7 consecutive days. If the testnet changes substantially, we'll require people to validate on the updated version of the testnet (but the goal there is only to ensure that we have working validators at launch). Here's an updated node. 
- should auth into Commonwealth (with your email or Github). We'll be communicating directly through Commonwealth and create a Telegram group for communications.
- should create a thread introducing yourself with positions on Edgeware governance and growth. In addition to bonding the EDG token at your address, it'll also be necessary for delegators to select with whom to delegate. This ensures enhanced security of the network. I'll link to the Commonwealth Labs answers, below. 

Here's the latest Edgeware-node -> https://github.com/hicommonwealth/edgeware-node

To set additional expectations, two important notes should be considered.

- **The first month should be considered betanet.** (In testnet 0.8.0, we'll trial using the council to turn on token transfers.)
- **We're planning on keeping token transfers *off* at launch, by setting the transfer fee to MAX_BLOCKS.** After two weeks to a month of stability, we'll create a signaling proposal to activate transfers. This should be an exciting first test of Edgeware governance.

title: What to do with WithdrawDAO's Signaled Funds
body:
### Summary

We have no issues with the WithdrawDAO signal as it was a case of open contract participation.

Since we can reasonably believe the original signaler intends for the allocated EDG to be disused, the community may decide to do something with the balance.

### **Background**

On July 2nd, 2019, Nick Johnson, the deployer of a contract called the WithdrawDAO signaled roughly ~123,000 ETH in the lockdrop.

Shortly afterward, he published the ETH private key for the contract deployer account, which allowed anyone to repeat his signal. He also announced he had destroyed his only copy of the EDG private key he had signaled:

> I used the account that deployed the DAO Withdrawal contract to signal on Edgeware. (...)

> I've deleted the only copy I had of the Edgeware private key. If Edgeware credits the account, those funds will now be locked permanently. As it's impossible to prove I really did delete the key, I encourage them not to credit it (or anyone else signaling for that matter)*

> I'm hereby publishing the private key for the account that deployed the DAO withdrawal contract: D6C8ACE470AB0CE03125CAC6ABF2779C199D21A47D3E75E93C212B1EC23CFE51.*

From https://twitter.com/nicksdjohnson/status/1146018815836164096

### Handling additional WithdrawDAO signals****

The lockdrop process took a snapshot of all signaled ETH balances at 00:00 UTC Sept 1. Signaled ETH accounts were checked *at that time only,* preventing users from shuffling ETH around, signaling, and shuffling again to a new address.

If multiple signals map the same ETH to different Edgeware addresses, the lockdrop process must decide which **EDG address should receive the allocation for that signal. This was not defined during the lockdrop process, because the code for creating a genesis spec had not been written.

Commonwealth decided to allow an ETH address to only be signaled **once. In this case, later signals would be ignored and only the first signal from the WithdrawDAO, from Nick Johnson
