title: The Evolution of Labor Groups in Edgeware
body:
**Summary: **This article is primarily a speculative vision for how the Working Groups may evolve over time, and helps inform the skill-tree model I proposed in the Games Working Group recently:
## 
## Stage 1: Working Group
**An unsustainable task force**
 Designed to  discover, investigate and plan an initial solution to a challenge, many working groups focus on increase awareness of the birth-chain, convert users and partners and generated use-cases.  Very 1-1 efforts, ad hoc tactics, and non-scaling conversions towards goals. Limited by resources including funding, people, and talent. 

Should a process for solving a challenge be discovered, and smaller grants by the birth-chain or other 3rd party be reliable, they may receive their own discretionary funding, enabling them to become an agency. 

Key Events:
- Formation
- Reaching 60 Group Participants
- Reaching 9-12 Core Members
- **Transformational Event: **Forms a multisig and receives funding.
- **Transformational Event: **200 participants.


_Example: Games Working Group, Artist Working Group_

## Stage 2: Agency / Firm
**A funds-redeployer contracting other workers and agencies **
A KPI-centric strategic board deploying funds seeking to measure return on those funds and optimize their use.  Discretionary funding from the birth-chain allows this entity to contract other agencies, contractors, and specialists on their own terms, rather than relying on scope-limited grants or bounties. Whether they wisely deploy their funding  determines whether they devolve to a Working Group, grow into their next stage, or cease operations. 

They may also engage in capacity building in order to in-source work or provide talent related to their initial mission to other peers or groups in the birth-chain’s ecosystem, but may also provide outsource talent at a premium.

title: Working Group: Finance & Econ. Commission
body:
As Edgeware is a DAO, we will need to plan for the management of various types assets, for expert opinion on financial proposals, and for a more robust understanding of Edgeware's economic model. 

Although I have drafted many support resources on this matter, including [staking ](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1VlzTUDESbbfOggMRz3GyE9-VqR9MlOhNuoekBboKvLw/edit#gid=2011072230)and [inflation estimators](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/1ghpu42zin), [supply curve charts](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1bKuD0GnQr-HZIrPdos6UuVBfOu27MxAuKqF5t2llOHM/edit#gid=0), [token economics pages](https://docs.edgewa.re/edgeware-runtime/economics), there is some uncertainty about the veracity of these - rightfully so, as I am _terrible _at math and have no background in these things other than my experience in crypto.  =-D 

**To that end, I propose the creation of a team of financial and economic thinkers to advise on strategies, propose asset management actions, analyze financial proposals, verify information, correct errors where prudent (staking estimates from 3rd parties being one item that comes to mind, or the functioning of estimators like Furqan recently gifted the community.)**

This "Working Group" will probably need to be more intentionally hired rather than volunteer base at least for the first 1-3 members.  I use the term commission here because it is an ongoing public good that requires prized talent, so the first step likely is to source a Group Lead / Chief Economist to coordinate and form reports. This person ideally has a background in both Dev and Finance/Econ, but a quantitative and technical mind is likely sufficient for resolving current unknowns and leading a group.

title: Requiring Signal Events prior to Referendums
body:
**Referencing Signal Event:[ EDG SIG 8](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/signalingproposal/0xe22b8fb78a0f099d294696532a8d809169989b135fbdc9b0d7728cebfb667e54-use-signaling-before-proposing-in-validator-set-changes)**


I think I am favor of a deliberative population obtaining a comprehensive signal about the views of others on a matter before they take it to binding referendum. 

For instance, you may approach a vote normally with the idea that 'my vote doesn't matter' but if you knew before that it was actually quite 50/50, you might vote differently or avoid 'protest votes.' I would take this a step further and say that our democratic process should FORCE a signaling event prior to referendum. 

Would love to hear views about why we wouldn't want this to be required at least some actions - speed is one, but if the tools the community is building to enhance gov (including this one!) work at compelling robust and consistent engagement,  I am all for shortening cycles.

title: Validator Economics
body:
Consolidating a few threads that have brought up validator economics. There’s been some recent discussion by community members around the economics of validating. The gist is that reward given to validators is too low, which seems important to address as we compete for a healthy validator ecosystem.

Overall, a large treasury, right now is a “feature”, rather than a bug. Its main use is to attract developers, a separate but equally important set of stakeholder. If there are no dapps or protocols to provide fees, the network atrophies over the long term. Even if the treasury is large now, I think we should weigh the potential effects on any changes that directly limit the treasury will have in the long run. Instead of trying to limit the treasury, the network can bring rewards in line with other networks without turning off the treasury reward.

TLDR. Easiest way to increase validator returns in line with other networks, while still maintaining the treasury is to lower **ideal staking rate from 80% to 50%, while maintaining the same over inflation to validators at 10%. This pushes up the overall interest rate to validators to 20% if the target 50% of the network is staked.**
Here, I’ll go over:

- Key parameters that influence validator rewards
- Preferred adjustment to incentivize validators (outlined above)
- Current thoughts on validator count / competition.


**What are the key parameters that influence validator returns (and where they are right now)?**

- Ideal Inflation Rate: The inflation rate that the network sets for validators (currently 10%). It feels unnecessary to increase this amount.
- Ideal Staking Rate: Currently 80%, which was derived by consulting [Web3 research docs on token economics](https://research.web3.foundation/en/latest/polkadot/Token%20Economics.html).
- Inflation Rate Function: If the network is below the ideal staking rate, then the interest paid to individual validators will be higher than the target 20%, which we can derive by taking

title: Edgeware as "Third Way" chain
body:
Vitalik had a semi-recent tweet about a "third way" chain that would take the political tradeoffs that ETH/BTC don't take. It seems like Edgeware is 1/3rd of the way there, with on-chain governance.




This was followed up by a thread on ethresear.ch on an [Enshrined Price Oracle](https://ethresear.ch/t/enshrined-eth2-price-feeds/7391), where validators would also offer this. It seemed like the consensus in that thread was not to move forward, but seems like an example of a feature that Edgeware as a community could implement and fund through the treasury.

As specified in the above thread, there is no economic slashing. If an enshrined price feed were implemented on Edgeware, the network could add economic slashing as well as additional rewards, where a subset of validators opt in to earn additional rewards by reporting this feed. This would probably have to be implemented as an additional runtime module.

I guess there are a few follow up thoughts / actions:
- [ ] Talking through chain positioning, and the feature set to continue building towards (I.e to extend governance)
- [ ] Understanding how this chain positioning impacts the sets of developers that we would be able to attract
- [ ] Specifically talk about the Enshrined Price Oracle. From a dev perspective, oracles are a perennial attack vector, especially for DeFi. Offering a solution baked into the chain seems very helpful. My main concerns would be if there is a dev team that could champion a discussion around the economics / development of such a proposal

Treasury Budget
body:
On the latest [governance call](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/461-may-community-call-summary-and-notes), there was a healthy discussion around how the treasury should be used. Hopefully, this thread can crystalize that conversation around “budgets" and further the conversation by proposing a governance process for approving such a budget.
## **Areas of Focus**

One of the core features of Edgeware outlined in the original whitepaper is the on-chain treasury. The goal for the treasury is to incentivize the development of network goods that users can provide.

Currently, the chain specifies a ~500m EDG to be minted directly to the treasury—a 10% increase from the initial supply in the first year. However, with unclaimed validator rewards going directly to the treasury, the treasury is running a “surplus”. This surplus arises when the percentage of the network staked is lower than the target (80%). In this case, an additional +5% of yearly inflation is going to the treasury. The budget discusses how both the 10% and additional surplus could be used.

**30% of treasury inflation - Core Development**: Making the chain attractive for developers by chain feature set. With many different pallets being developed by independent teams within the Substrate Ecosystem, it seems this will take the shape of Edgeware continuing to allocate grants to teams to help integrate their runtime and improvements to those pallets, or ground-up development.
- Projects include:
- [Integrating Runtime Bridges](https://wiki.polkadot.network/docs/en/learn-bridges#runtime-module-bridges)
- Additional Runtime Audits
- Bug Bounty Program
- Social Key Recovery Pallet
- Cumulus Runtime Integration
- EVM and Contracts Module Support
- Alternative client implementations


**20% of treasury inflation - DOT Bond**: For Edgeware to bid for a parachain slot, it will need to acquire DOTs. While the mechanics of this are still a bit unclear, it would coincide with Polkadot network launch

title: Edgeware Release Naming Tournament
body:
We're excited to open a conversation on release naming for Edgeware. As many networks have conveniently named releases that help users understand what versions they are interacting with, we want to take the opportunity to create a process- and a game, for selecting these. To begin, we're advocating for the use of international city names to track Edgeware's progress.

_**Why are we choosing cities?**_

- Cities are bottom-up, resilient and emergent structures.
- They are also cooperative collectives and economies.
- Cities grow over time.
- They welcome all new-comers.
- City names are memorable, accessible and inspiring.

## The Naming Tournament
We're proposing that we hold 2 rounds of signaling polls where 1-account-1-vote applies, starting with 3 4-choice polls of the cities found below. The top winner of each set continues onto the next until the order according to most winning is discovered. The higher the # of accounts voting for that release, the later the named release, ensuring that our favorite names represent the most advanced versions of Edgeware.  While this does open the door for sybil attacks via 1-a-1-v, the matter is thankfully more fun than serious. 

Barring any issues, we aim to launch this process this coming **Tuesday,  June 23. **

title: Edgeware Upgrade Update
body:
# The Latest
Alexander from Parity and I have been compiling migrations and updating the node against substrate master. Since we started more than 1 month ago, we've gathered a number of migrations related to balances, hashers, staking, and accounts — a total of 8 migrations. Additionally, we've updated the node many times against the substrate master branch and are continuously testing the upgrade flows for networks with old and new nodes before and after an upgrade. As this maintenance project is composed of integrating changes across 4 months of active work on Substrate, it is quite substantial and has been a very time-intensive process.

# Functional Changes
### Staking
For the staking migration, future changes will impact the payout schemes for nominators and validators. We will move to a simple payout scheme that is now live on Kusama/Substrate where validators can claim payouts for themselves and their nominators in one flow.

### Iterable Storage Maps
From the opaque hashes migration, Edgeware storage maps will now be iterable which was previously unavailable. This is a nice feature to have for any projects building on Edgeware as it allows them to search through maps directly without directly knowing keys for key/value pairs.

## Remaining work
The remaining migrations are tracked [here](https://github.com/hicommonwealth/edgeware-node/issues/164). For the balances migration we will also need to collect every Edgeware account to migrate the storage locations of balances. This task is ongoing and will begin more extensive work next week.
Once we collect all migrations, we will undergo a period of testing these changes on local networks to ensure that there is a stable path for old and new node operators when these changes take effect on Mainnet.

_**- Drew Stone**_

title: New website
body:
OK! So, as I promised in the Edgeware Brand Working Group, here is a little text summarizing my thoughts regarding what should be done in the near future, in regards with the Edgeware brand.

## Website

The website really needs to be refreshed. And the reason why I think so is mainly because if you currently go on the website, you will just think of Edgeware as again, another smart contract blockchain. 

The problem is that there are tens, if not hundreds of smart contract blockchains out there, which all failed. So how is Edgeware different. How is it not going to fail?

You can't convince people that Edgeware is not going to fail, if you bring the arguments to the table our competitors use. 

And the arguments our competitors bring to the table are pretty simple: scalability, interoperability, decentralization, security,...

But guess what? People don't care about that. What people care about is how this product is going to change their lives for the better. How is Edgeware going to improve your life? How is it different from all the other blockchains out there?

So, how should the website look like?

## How the website should look like

In my opinion, the main page should be very minimal. A bit like [Ethereum](https://ethereum.org)'s website. It needs to be very minimal, and people need to quickly understand what Edgeware is about.

So in my opinion, the "key ideas", "lockdrop", "edgeware stack", and even "about Commonwealth labs" parts should be removed. 

The only thing on the page, should be a little paragraph, ideally just a phrase, summarizing what Edgeware is about. Like on Ethereum's website. 

Just under, there should be 4 links. 

### Use Edgeware

The first link should bring users to a page where they can learn more about using Edgeware, which projects are currently building Edgeware,... Essentially, the Edgeware ecosystem. While this will likely be very little currently, it will hopefully grow as time goes.

title: Why Edgeware? Pros and Cons of Parachains versus Smart Contract Platforms
body:
# 
From [my article posted to Medium](https://medium.com/@thom_iv/why-edgeware-pros-and-cons-of-parachains-versus-smart-contract-platforms-d879bcb91049), I offer this up for workshopping by the community and for information.
# Why go Edgeware?
## Turn-Key Community
- Tap into an existing community of validators, holders, stakers, and governance participants instead of managing an entire chain’s community, letting you focus on your use-case and finding fit.
- You have the option to manage your governance stack more simply by participating in Edgeware instead of growing and. managing a parachain governance system (plus monitoring relay-chain governance) by relying on a community of similarly-positioned developers to share the work.
- Share in the technical support community and documentation of an existing chain.
- [Nested parachains are possible](https://medium.com/polkadot-network/polkadot-the-parachain-3808040a769a) — Edgeware may someday launch relaychain functionality, making transitions from dapp-to-chain more fluid, token-incentive aligned, and maintaining your community and ecosystem of tools.
- Additionally, nested parachains repurpose validator infrastructure and node operators, who historically provide development tools, promotional efforts and more. When becoming a parachain, validators are no longer required because of the shared security model of the relaychain.


## Test Before You Invest
- Launch, test, and scale on Edgeware while you consider whether to pursue a parachain and an appropriate token-economic model for that chain.
- No slot auctions. Existing on a parachain doesn’t cost tokens to bond for limited slots, and you can never be removed from the ecosystem after that claim expires. You also don’t have to convince relay-chain token holders like DOT holders to participate in your crowdfunding on your behalf.


## Flexible, functional, friendly.

body:
## About Blockx Labs

We are a team of blockchain developers with expertise in building developer tools and an enjoyment of open source projects. You can check out our work at our [Github ](https://github.com/blockxlabs/).  We are also the developers behind the testnet Edgeware faucet, and are familiar with the network through our work on wallets and dapp explorers.

We have built Enzyme - a browser extension wallet for Substrate-based chains, currently supporting Kusama and Polkadot. It can be downloaded for [Chrome ](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/enzyme/amligljifngdnodkebecdijmhnhojohh?hl=en)and[ Firefox](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/enzyme). 

The wallet allows the user to: 
1. Check balances 
2. Send & receive tokens 
3. Allow DApps to sign messages 
4. Use an address book built to improve the user experience.


We have had several discussions with the Commonwealth team over the year about both our faucet and extending the wallet functionality to support the Edgeware network. With the wallet development wrapping up, we’re looking to finalize the integration of EDG to provide options for users in the Substrate ecosystem, but also to forward our view of a more modular approach to wallet development.

**A browser extension wallet is essential in creating a DApp community for any network.** Without a browser extension wallet, DApps can’t access the private key functionalities including signing, and this interferes with a smooth user experience.  Having an extension-based wallet similar to Metamask will enhance both the holder and developer experience.

title: Gantree Integration for all Edgeware validators
body:
In a recent call with the Gantree team, I learned about their monitoring tool and future work extending it to a robust system for validators. In short, Gantree is building a node monitoring system that integrates with Substrate blockchains and provides individual and network level node statistics around node health, uptime, and more. I think it's a great project to onboard into our ecosystem and have an interesting idea how we do so.

## Service Partners
Gantree's service will likely be a monthly subscription service paid out based on the number of nodes you integrate. They may offer unlimited node service for a fixed monthly cost and small additional cost per node. This makes it quite appealing to fund entirely through the Treasury for ALL Edgeware node operators. In this sense, we could fund operations of Gantree for every Edgeware node operator, funded by the Treasury.

I see this potential partnership as a network-wide service partner as we could potentially negotiate for a network-wide agreement. This would benefit all current and future Edgeware node operators and validators by providing them tools, paid for by the Treasury, to help them manage and understand both their current node infrastructure as well how to improve their infrastructure.

One potential way we do this, is by utilising the streaming reward or scheduled payments to Gantree for the course of 6 months or a year. Defining a service agreement would allow us to pay once and for all potentially for a service that any node operator of Edgeware will benefit from. This model sounds super appealing for a blossoming chain like Edgeware and is a novel way to both support and integrate service providers like Gantree into the Edgeware ecosystem.

Would love to hear if people find this interesting and if we would like to continue the discussion further with Gantree.

title: Lessons from Decred on governance, community culture and proposals
body:
Hi all. So had brief chat with Dillon in the EDG design / brand telegram group. I'm a participant in the lockdrop and am fascinated by the opportunity around DAOs with sustainable funding that can help coordinate global talent pools across a wide range of disciplines.

I am also a long time member of the Decred community and have been focused most recently on solving many of the issues around brand building, narrative development and community culture that Edgeware are currently discussing. Something that Decred has been testing ideas around since 2018. 

For those not aware, Decred was inspired by issues the core development team saw with Bitcoin.

1. Centralisation of miners and overall security (solved with a hybrid PoW/PoS system) (60% of block rewards go to miners, 30% to those staking who also validate blocks)
2. Sustainable funding - the remaining 10% pool to a [treasury](https://explorer.dcrdata.org/address/Dcur2mcGjmENx4DhNqDctW5wJCVyT3Qeqkx). This will soon be fully [decentralised](https://proposals.decred.org/proposals/c96290a2478d0a1916284438ea2c59a1215fe768a87648d04d45f6b7ecb82c3f). 
3. Governance - they created the Politeia proposal system and [contractor management system](https://github.com/decred/contractor-mgmt). 


I wrote this [Forks In The Road](https://github.com/monsieurbulb/forksintheroad/blob/master/Decred_forks_in_the_road.md) paper about the challenges the project has faced and thought it might be useful to share here. Chris Burniske (an investor in both Decred and Polkadot projects) shared his thoughts [here](https://twitter.com/cburniske/status/1265104775550570498?s=20). 

My belief is that coordination of sustainable on-chain treasuries and cross-chain governance is a necessary precursor to tacking the tribalism present in crypto - enabling communities to work together for the common good, rather than engaging in endless (and pointless) spats. 

Would love any thoughts.

title: Edgeware 2020 - Roadmap Discussion
body:

title: builDAO: Incubator Discussion Thread
body:
Hey all, this has been circulating in the chats for quite some time. I wanted to open this thread here so we can add any comments directly below here.

In short, we think we can quickly bootstrap network adoption on the developer side by creating an on chain incubator. We think this incubator can should be focused on two key use case cases--DeFi and crypto social. As a community we have potential distribution to over 13m users, as well as people that want to experiment with different new projects. There is an existing playbook for distribution and building demand in DeFi that we can also learn from. On the legal side, Edgeware could hold tokens as well as equity in different "real world" entities by creating corporate form (a Delaware LLC).

We think this could be seeded by the Edgeware Treasury ($250k - $500k) to create a legally linked entity. We have also chatted with the Polkdot Treasury members, and think that this something that could see wide spread Polkadot ecosystem adoption.

A future form of builDAO could allow people to add assets along a bonding curve, creating a "permanent capital" incubator or fund.

title: MetaDAO - pooling on-chain funding for public good proposals
body:
There is a phrase:

> [A rising tide lifts all boats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_rising_tide_lifts_all_boats)

It is a term associated with the idea that an improved economy will benefit all participants.

Right now there is an opportunity for a certain group of projects to benefit from the (crypto) mainstreaming of DAOs with **sustainable funding**, **governance via proposal systems** and **decentralised contributions.**

This narrative is well underway as evidenced by the last couple of months hype/speculation around 'governance tokens' and more specifically the arrival of [Substrate](https://substrate.dev/) based chains, all of which have their own treasuries, governance and multi-million $ treasuries.

For most people, the first generation of DAOs primarily consisted of DAOstack, Moloch and Aragon - an area that has failed to live up to adoption expectations.

All have all been donation / individual based and therefore are not sustainable in nature since there is no perpetual funding mechanism of the sort pioneered by [Decred](https://decred.org) that gives the ability to invest consistently over the long term.

The number of projects with self-sustaining on-chain treasuries will increase exponentially over the next 12 months with [Cosmos SDK](https://cosmos.network/sdk) being the base for Aragon's [own chain](https://aragon.org/chain).

This also doesn't include existing projects with treasuries / founder rewards such as DASH and ZCash, whose issues with transparency and impact have been noted [elsewhere.](https://medium.com/@richardred/observations-of-the-dash-treasury-dao-c94231b2b5c4)

## **The tribalism dilemma**
Tokens naturally inspire tribalism - since greed / price discussion dominates the conversation and actually distracts from much of the progress made in the space.

However, the broader shared goal for credible project teams is in building a fairer, more decentralised future that offers users better control and coordination of their information

title: Bereshet Testnet Launched!
body:
As we approach the mainnet Edgeware upgrade to Substrate 2.0 rc3, we want to give an update of the recent work that's gone on. Most of which has culminated in a new testnet, called Beresheet (meaning "in the/a beginning").

This testnet runs off the version 3.0.8 Edgeware node, recently pushed to release in a testnet mode. We have yet to push this release to the master branch and will do so soon. We plan to run this testnet for as long as the community finds desirable before moving forward with the upgrade.

This testnet was launched at the beginning of the week of August 2nd with the same genesis spec as Edgeware. The only changes are to the initial validator set which Commonwealth Labs maintains at the moment. Once the chain was launched, it was left running for a few days before running our pending runtime upgrade. This was run early to ensure we have a few weeks or longer to test out the upgraded chain, its functionality, and more. There was feedback from the community that was well received and will inform how we can do a better job around these upgrades in the future.
Namely,
- Larger announcement of testnet prior to running a runtime upgrade.
- Incentivization of node infrastructure for the testnet.
- There are some early ideas here, but this probably looks like getting tipped from the Edgeware Treasury with various milestones for continued tips/payments.


With that said, we want to open up an validators-only announcements channel to keep people upgraded on node updates and new testnets. If validators are able to add their on-chain identity and Telegram or Riot name, we can add individuals.

Nonetheless, we are interested to get more participation on the testnet, deploy contracts, and get feedback about how it is working currently. We are working to smooth out any rough edges at the moment too!

title: Release Naples · hicommonwealth/edgeware-node · GitHub
body:
## Overview 
With the upcoming runtime upgrade to Edgeware mainnet, there is a need to coordinate a node upgrade with validators and node operators. When and if the runtime upgrade is passed and enacted, all old and outdated Edgeware nodes will not function properly out-of-the-box.

To that end, we will need everyone to upgrade their nodes to version 3.0.8 that is now in release for Edgeware Mainnet on Github. Running the 3.0.8 can be configured with some extra parameters to sync the chain faster and reduce lagging at the end of eras. These configuration settings are in the following doc:

[https://github.com/hicommonwealth/edgeware-node/releases/tag/v3.0.8](https://github.com/hicommonwealth/edgeware-node/releases/tag/v3.0.8)

## Proposal Plan
When 90%+ of nodes on mainnet begin running the new node v3.0.8, then we will push the upgrade through the democracy system.
For nodes that have not upgraded, we will apply the judgement below.

## Slash reimbursement positioning
There has been a decent amount of conversation around the nodes stalling as operators upgrade their setups, and so we want to address our positioning in the event that there are issues before and after upgrade.

So far all upgraded nodes are working quite well, without issues on the existing mainnet network. They are producing blocks, not stalling with the right configuration, and don't seem to be producing any issues. However, after running the upgrade this may not hold. Obviously, we will have to wait and find out.

**The case in which Commonwealth supports reimbursement / cancelling of slashes is if:**

- Node operators upgraded their nodes and experienced issues immediately after upgrade.


**Commonwealth maintains the position that we will not reimburse funds for slashes or vote to cancel them if:**

- Node operators do not upgrade their nodes in a reasonable period of time ~2 weeks.

title: A Crypto-way to manage Translation Work
body:
Occasionally we get inbound requests from would-be translators of EDG content. 
Given that we fund these sorts of network developments and supports using the public fund of the Treasury, we should ponder the best way to structure these engagements. 

For example:

Translator 1 wants to translate a document for some EDG into Mandarin. They apply for a grant and show their previous experience and other writing samples. Their grant is funded and they complete the task.

However, later on, a user or another translator reads the document and finds errors.

**How do we verify the work of would-be translators in a way befitting of the cryptoeconomic space?**

Overall, I would like this process to be
- Permissionless as possible, to reduce friction to expanding access to documentation and knowledge.
- Decentralized, so that no individual is burdened with coordinating these.
- Incentivized, so that translators step forward and perform
- Quality-controlled, so errors are avoided.
- Larger-scale, so we are not funding piecemeal translations of single or few blog articles, but rather large chunks of our written material.
- Sustainable, and designed so that translators are inclined to remain with the project into the future, that these relationships are a public good.



**Some proposed ideas:**

- Translation grants must have two translators who are paired, one to translate and one to verify or editorialize.  
- Translators must stake EDG or reputation to obtain a grant (this is already somewhat true for treasury proposals-- the proposer must bond a percentage of the amount looking to be received or a minimum EDG, whichever is larger) 
- Translators must provide verifiable letters of referral regarding the quality of their work.


I haven't yet had a moment to research how other teams do these- KSM may have some of the best guidance.

## Summary:
I am proposing 3-10 Artist Residencies funded by the Treasury, to support and disseminate Edgeware's values and mission.


## Growing a Polyculture: Artist Residencies

My work has largely been to grow the community of Edgeware - we've tried many different strategies over time, and now that Edgeware has launched we're approaching new tools that we can test. The strongest of these thus far has been the Treasury.

My strategy for bootstrapping the community recently has been the deployment and nurturing of a set of working groups and support the resourcing and coordination of these groups until they are self-sustaining. 

At the same time, I also watch and listen carefully to the explicated values of the users in order to find the 'ground floor' of Edgeware; the core tenants that unite the community. We've recently begun work at the BWG on drafting a constitution of sorts - which we are currently terming the 'Architecture.'

Whereas many chains begin with a monoculture, I am explicitly rejecting that path in favor of a robust polyculture: that Edgeware should have a diverse field of groups supporting different values, experimenting in different ways, and proving their needs and results to better access resourcing- for example through treasury grants.

Working groups are permissionless. Anyone may start one- and I would like to see many more: NFTs, Gaming, Token Engineering, DAOs are some that come to mind. In brief, I believe they allow others to collaborate on common goals, immediately find like-minded peers within our ecosystem, and support the growth of specific industries through co-support within Edgeware.

To build onto this infrastructure of a polyculture, I am proposing that we fund several Residencies or (should these be successful, longer term fellowships) native to the chain. title: Motivating Edgeware "Power" Members
body:
Summary: We have a few levers to pull to ensure our most contributing users remain involved and even more passionate. We need to begin designing those subsystems and tooling and I explore the options here.
--

Recently we discussed more appropriate names for Edgeware users - which is a very Web2, cold way to go about describing someone who participates in the system, which is also a DAO in the case of Edgeware.

I'm a fan of 'membership' in Edgeware, because it requires you to have some stake in the network. Now, this doesn't need to be purely token-holding, but it can also be reputation, and I expect we will integrate reputational tools ASAP since we already have an on-chain ID system that is primed to demonstrate more than just our attested IDs. 

I'm also interested in **micro-bounties**, where tasks are so divided into sub-tasks that we can offer an Amazon Turk-like experience, rewarding EDG from collective pools (like a Working Group budget,) or even the Treasury. 

In all communities, there needs to be a level of influential, highly contributing members. They model community values and norms through behavior, co-enforce these norms --and I want to say we should always use a call-in, rather than call-out culture to enforce these. 

But we cannot be transactional in our approach for many reasons- the first being that it's generally a perverse incentive in that it funds members who are potentially not aligned on value and mission, risks their termination of support when the incentive ends, and there are also legal liability concerns with volunteer programs that begin to look like tit-for-tat. (Something that chain-contractorships clearly butt up against but haven't been tested in any jurisdiction given the nature of blockchains.)

We should begin to consider upgrades to our ID module to leverage better platforming of power members as I mentioned above. Pride and accomplishments are massive drivers; social recognition. Specifically, these might involve avatar over

title: Edgeware 'rate cards' - aka how to value contributions?
body:
[@Thom Ivy](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/account/iJFChQEmukA7CNckr7TLZBjp4QxMxugEnzUVjceaJbPK9Sp) has outlined a range of interesting[ active proposals](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/538-active-proposals-and-status), [BuilDAO](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/534-buildao-treasury-request) had 50m EDG approved, there is discussion around motivating '[Power Members](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/539-motivating-edgeware-power-members)' alongside the coordination of [Working Groups](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/373-introducing-edgeware-working-groups) and areas such as [translation](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/532-a-cryptoway-to-manage-translation-work) that require dedicated contributions. 

Something that will soon become a challenge is: **how do you value a contribution? **

This ties to another area which is how to set 'fair' rates across a project in terms of the various roles, responsibilities and expected rates (if indeed rates are to be set). 

This also links to how proposals are budgeted, how costs are tracked and how value for money is demonstrated with clear deliverables. 

This is not something that will be solved immediately, but should be front of mind for everyone requesting funds from the treasury and for those managing the disbursement of those funds. 

**Why develop rate cards?**

If there is no consistency with how and why people are paid and against what deliverables, trust and transparency will be impossible to build. 

Historically companies withheld the amount they paid to different team members, even if they were doing the same jobs or had very similar roles. 

Over time this lack of transparency inevitably leads to internal cultural conflict (people talk) and over time tends to lead to a small cohort controlling the 'pricing' of labour or expenses and tending to extract increasing value.

body:
Hey community and Commonwealth Labs team, what do you think about relaunch of chain? Not immediately , but after some period like Cosmos had - Game of stakes, which was incentivized testnet run with a lot of performance testing. It can holds for e.g. 1-2 months and helps to find more potential issues, reward people who find out bugs, and more for the people who will fix them and then launch the mainnet. Substrate is extremely complex piece of tech and still in very early stage, so I see harder testing on testnet (incentivized with outstanding allocation 2.5% for testnet users, early adopters,etc.) then relaunch as a better option than trying to fix all bugs  / issues which happened to many people these days on mainnet ex post. I know that "core devs" are working as hard as possible to fix current problems, but there will be more of them (edge cases, instabilities, bad implementation not just by them, but for example from Parity, etc.) in the next months with EDG listed on exchanges and causing economic and PR troubles, which we can avoid. 

Even if you disagree with relaunch we should open discussion about establishing clear rules for a bug bounty program, rewarding reporting / fixing issues by community. Effort of many people playing with tech and helping with debugging is extremely important for the further development of network (sounds like captain obvious, but we should not forget about it).

title: [Cross-Post] Relaunch: Clean Genesis for Edgeware
body:
[This was cross-posted from the Edgeware blog](https://blog.edgewa.re/relaunch-clean-genesis-for-edgeware/)

===
The Edgeware mainnet soft-launched this past weekend, and since then, the network has produced over 20,000 blocks, finalized its first blocks, and proceeded through many rounds of validator rotations. We’ve also observed a number of issues with the network’s initial configuration.
 
The Edgeware community has acted quickly to identify these issues, and at this point, we think the long-term benefit of the network would be best served by relaunching with a clean genesis spec:
 
- It would be possible to use the soft-launch governance system to correct the genesis balances, reverse any slashings and balance transfers, and restore the treasury to its correct genesis balance.
- At that point, a script could be published to verify the state of the network against the (corrected) genesis spec. However, this would mean the network would continue to operate with an unclean original genesis. Over the long term, we think this would introduce more uncertainty than it benefits any participant in the network.
 
The steps we recommend include:
 
1. Downgrading the current network (launched on Sept 15th 00:00 UTC) to a testnet

title: Edgeware: Relaunch Plan
body:
Over the last week, we’ve had a series of conversations with validators, developers, and other community members around the rebooted mainnet launch of Edgeware. We’re grateful for the continued enthusiasm and patience, and for the advice that we’ve gotten. Now, we’re writing to share our next steps, and a rough timeline.

Starting this week, we’ll launch another testnet. Assuming it behaves as expected over the next 2-4 weeks, we will then move towards a full mainnet launch. During that time, we’ll be conducting extensive testing to ensure that all of the issues from the first mainnet launch, confirmed or unconfirmed, are resolved.

At the same time, we’ll be investing in stronger community engagement, including resources for validators and nominators. (Thanks to those who provided input to this process already, including soc1c, Florian from Staking Facilities, and melea.trust. Florian has also published a document of recommendations which we have incorporated in large part.)

### Our checklist for relaunch

- Operate a stable testnet for 2-4 weeks
- Onboard at least ten new validator nodes, from at least five community members
- Ensure there are no unexpected slashing events
- Conduct at least two runtime upgrades without issues
- Allow new validators to join the mainnet genesis set, if they have participated in the testnet.

Once all the above steps are done, we will generate a recommended mainnet spec and share it with the community. This will happen with at least three days’ lead time before launch.

title: How can we fix tribalism in cryptocurrency?
body:
At Berlin Blockchain Week '19 last month, Commonwealth’s Chief-of-Staff Thom Ivy sat down with Gavin Wood for a chat on governance in the blockchain space. The discussion began with the subject of tribalism, a topic well-known to many in this community. Tribalism is listed as one of the “ten dark secrets of crypto” according to an article at Hackernoon [1], and you can even download a browser extension built to *identify* tribalism when it appears subtly on Twitter, called “Coinflict of Interest.” [2] As Gavin iterated in his chat with Thom, tribalism is problematic, and it needs to stop - but ending that tribalism is no simple task.

The most common and extreme case of tribalism is that of Bitcoin maximalism. Bitcoin maximalists don’t *just* think Bitcoin is a superior coin-they believe that no other coin should exist - or nearly any other use of blockchain technology, for that matter, and if it should, Bitcoin will eventually do it. We saw this argument play out between Ethereum and Polkadot more recently: "Eth2 will solve that use case," is a trope, noted 1Confirmation. [3]

This maximalist belief is often acted out in fairly distasteful ways. Last week, noted Bitcoin maximalist Matt Odell started posting on Twitter calling for donations of altcoins to the TOR project, writing “donate shitcoins. stack sats.” [4] Many Bitcoin maximalists jumped at the chance to use donations to the project as a way to dump their "shitcoins" - and took every opportunity to make it clear that their donation was not about TOR, but instead was strictly for the purpose of getting rid of the altcoins that they think of as worthless.

Tribalism generally takes the form of talking up one’s own network or attacking a different network. The attacks can get personal, and they can get really nasty. The problem isn't limited to Bitcoin holders; Ethereum Maximalists are starting to emerge, as admitted even by one of Ethereum’s co-founders, Joseph Lubin, now founder of Consensys. This is a diffi

title: Implementing Social Key Recovery
body:
What is Social Key Recovery?

Social Key Recovery is a tactic for getting back a lost password that is based on Shamir’s Secret Sharing Scheme (SSSS). You might have already heard of HTC’s cryptocurrency phone, Exodus, putting it into practice, or perhaps their app, Zion. The idea is basically that you can share your password among friends, and if you lose your key, your friends can help you out. Social Key Recovery is an easy-to-use system that could become an integral part of Edgeware for ensuring account security and access in extraordinary circumstances (which could range from unavailability of the main key, to death of the main password holder).


How does Shamir's Secret Sharing Scheme work?

SSSS allows for a secret to be split and defines a threshold number of individuals required to put it back together. With this mechanism, there is no single point-of-failure. If you shared your secret with three people, then you would need two of them to confirm your identity and deliver your secret back to you. For the key recovery use case, your secret is your secondary key, which you can split into “shards” and distribute to other trusted persons using a linear key split.

You have the option to choose how many shards you want and who to give them to. It would make sense to give your shards to different types of friends and family. You wouldn’t want to give three of your four shards to your business partners, for instance, because then they may be more likely to collude against you. The more shards you make and the more trusted contacts you introduce, the more secure your recovery key is.

Christopher Allen and Mark Friedenbach, authors of a commonly cited article on the topic that was written in January of this year, suggest calling these different types of trusted contacts “circles.” They further suggest allowing the user to specify different thresholds for each circle (so you might need just one business partner, but two family members to put together your recovery

title: EOS Vote-Buying and Power Distribution
body:
Last week, Daniel Larimer, founder of EOS blockchain, posted a Tweet saying that he and co-founder Brendan Blumer “came up with an amazing solution to vote buying,” and the EOS governance *will* be decentralized - which some took as a confession that the network has never been decentralized. [1] EOS has always had issues with power distribution - though whether those issues are actually on their way to being solved remains to be seen.

**Is EOS decentralized?**

Since its beginning, the EOS blockchain has been plagued by critiques of its governance structure, with many voicing concerns that the network’s power distribution is problematic on a number of levels. For those unfamiliar, EOS blockchain is the network made by Block.One in 2017 and uses a delegated Proof-of-Stake model. It’s a massive network - as of February 2019, it was the world’s seventh largest blockchain by market value, which is more than 3 billion USD.[2]

The network is set up so that the top 21 Block Producers (BPs) receive coins (EOS) for block production according to their rank, but are also elected by EOS holders whose votes are weighted proportionally to their holdings. This has created a system where BPs can use their EOS to buy votes, getting themselves higher in the ranking and earning more tokens to continue the unfair power cycle.

To even get into that top 21 rank, a huge amount of EOS is required (as of last week, the minimum amount was over 256 million and the BP at the top 310 million tokens with a daily profit of almost 1000 EOS). [3] There are also around 50 standby BPs who earn revenue in this capacity, with all BPs sharing a portion of EOS tokens’ annual 1% inflation.

Block.One itself holds the largest amount of coins, meaning that any BPs would theoretically need its vote to be approved, should Block.One choose to vote - but so far, the company has yet to take any actions at all.

Governance and power has been an issue for EOS from the very beginning. One of the first moves ever

title: How to Fund Dev Tools for Blockchains
body:
Building good, useful development tools is necessary for blockchain success, but it also requires funding - and it can be hard to ensure developers get the resources they need without a clear plan for supporting long-term innovation and development in a network.

**What are some funding options that have been explored for dev tools?**

Grants are one of the most common ways to get funding for building. Web3 and the Ethereum Community Fund are some of the biggest entities in this space offering grants to those who apply. Aragon, which at the time of writing was listed at number five on the State of the dApps ranking for chains with the most development activity in September 2019, also introduced the Aragorn Nest program in 2017 to facilitate grants for those looking to further development of the network. The Nest program works with a venture capital firm called Placeholder.

**How could sustainable development for a chain be driven by the community?**

One option for using a native currency to fund development that the Stellar network has implemented is an inflation pool that funds projects by user choice.

The Stellar protocol has an inflation mechanism that adds 1% inflation of Lumens (XLM) to the pool each year. Users can vote to use money from the inflation pool to support different projects that they believe are significant for the Stellar network. If a user votes for a project, the project will receive 1% of that wallet, to be distributed every week.

It isn’t quite so simple as being able to donate inflation money to a project you think is worthy, though. A project won’t actually receive inflation pool money unless it reaches a certain amount of tokens designated for it. Because the inflation mechanism only allows 1% of the wallet to be donated, it actually requires many people to put their “inflation votes” and the attached XLM amount towards that project to meet the minimum token threshold.

title: Semaphore and the Potential for a Private DAO
body:
Currently, it is still possible to connect an individual’s actions within a DAO, even if all the members are anonymous. For those concerned with total privacy, this is obviously an issue. Semaphore is a solution to this problem: a language that was built to create smart contracts that allow for anonymous signaling and solve the problem of DAO privacy.

**How does Semaphore work?**

The Semaphore smart contract allows anyone to make a proposal, so long as they verify their identity as a member of the group. The smart contract requires a unique nullifier (for each proposal to have a unique identification), and an epoch to be specified (this helps avoid spam proposals). Members can use external_nullifier = hash(proposal_id) to make a Semaphore signal and vote once on each proposal. A snark is used to prove membership of a merkle tree and calculate the nullifier.

The circuit uses a burn relay to refund users the gas money it takes to participate. To create a proposal, you pay a proposal fee, which is then used to pay the gas for everyone who votes on it. They then propose using [Burn relay registry: Decentralized transaction abstraction on layer 2](https://ethresear.ch/t/burn-relay-registry-decentralized-transaction-abstraction-on-layer-2/5820) (you can see the code for this at [https://github.com/lsankar4033/micromix_relayer](https://github.com/lsankar4033/micromix_relayer)).

Although Semaphore solves the problem of action-anonymity, it still runs the risk of votes being subject to collusion. While private DAO created with Semaphore is indeed private, the author of the introduction to the language barryWhiteHat is quick to point out that the individual can still prove the content of their vote. This creates a very real potential for vote-buying or other forms of collusion.

[See the code for the Semaphore circuit here.](https://github.com/kobigurk/semaphore.)

**Why should a DAO be private?**

The Semaphore circuit has already been built, it’s just waiting for a DAO

title: The Implications of Dark DAOs
body:
**The Problem of Dark DAOs**

Philip Daian and his team’s paper “On-Chain Vote Buying and the DAO Dark Ages” set off a string of reactionary pieces, including his own follow up post. In the original article, the authors explicated an attack infrastructure that showed that any network that uses on-chain voting is susceptible to vote-buying, and argued that smart contracts, trusted hardware, and anonymity would allow for the creation of Dark DAOs: groups that specifically engage in vote-buying for some (usually financial) gain. 

According to the paper, not only does the structure of on-chain governance systems allow for vote-buying, but there are several elements that encourage it. First, while anyone who holds coins theoretically sees overall network utility as an ultimate goal, factors like the possibility for more and/or earlier financial gain could incentivize vote-selling anyways - especially if participants are able to easily leave a network. Daian and company also note that Oracles (like Town Crier, multiple oracles, or prediction markets) can be used to simplify the vote-buying process by mapping real-world information and supplying it to chains (Daian et al., 2018).

In Daian’s personal followup article on the topic, he describes how quadratic voting increases the probability of vote-buying and Dark DAO attacks. Quadratic voting is meant to decrease the possibility for plutocracy by implementing a system where the cost of votes increases exponentially. However, Daian makes the point that if the system depends on user-generated key-based identities, then a wealthy individual could simply split their identity and leverage their wealth to sway the vote.

title: Crowdsourcing the Public Good: Dominant Assurance Contracts
body:
**What is a Dominant Assurance Contract?**

Assurance contracts are a product of game theory that seek to manage the “free rider problem.” The free rider problem describes a situation in which somebody might not personally contribute to the creation of a public good that would benefit the whole community, but could still reap the rewards of others’ contributions.

A simple assurance contract, also called a provision point mechanism, ensures that members of a group are bound to their contribution to a public good, as long as some contribution threshold is met (say, a specified number of contributors or amount of money). If the threshold isn’t met, all of the contributed money is refunded. This creates an incentive to contribute in the first place - either you get the public good, or you get your money back. It’s a win-win.

A Dominant Assurance Contract (DAC) is an assurance contract with a refund system built in to incentivize participation even more. In a Dominant Assurance Contract, the individual who offers the public good (the entrepreneur) pays the contributors a refund bonus if the contribution threshold is not met. If the threshold is met, the public good is created and the entrepreneur gets a bit of profit. This way if the contract is executed the entrepreneur is rewarded for the risk of creating such a contract, and if the contract fails to execute the contributors are rewarded a bonus for participating (Tabarrok).

The creator of DACs, Alex Tabarrok, believed that this contract set up would make participation in funding the public good the dominant choice for members of a community, as they would perceive a lack of risk and be excited by the potential for reward. The DAC theoretically creates a situation in which the contract would almost always gain the participation necessary to pass the contribution threshold.

**How do you decide how much to refund contributors?**

This is where it gets tricky.

title: Examining the Edgeware Lockdrop: Gini coefficients and successes.
body:
Thank you to everyone for participating in the on-going experiment that is the Edgeware network. When we started the lockdrop process, we didn’t anticipate how many would take part, now with the lockdrop closed, we want to highlight a few of our takeaways. While there have been some edge-cases, that’s the nature of cutting-edge experiments and we’re excited to get people thinking about variations in the solutions to these challenges.

**Overall**
The total ETH locked in the standard process finalized at 1,199,728 ETH, with signaled funds at 4,346,544 ETH. This demonstrates strong confidence and interest in both the contracts underlying the lockdrop, but also the advance in blockchain technology that Edgeware represents. Today there exist over 4000 different Edgeware addresses largely created in the lockdrop process, from over 10,000 transactions. 

The lockdrop mechanism was primarily designed to distribute a utility token in a more decentralized and equal fashion while strongly selecting for committed users and holders, this was achieved by ‘supercharging’ the power of small amounts by allowing for the use of time as leverage: lock longer, get more.

body:
Web3 Foundation awards grants to teams with amazing projects that fit within the Polkadot ecosystem. This past August, they awarded most Wave 3 grants to projects that focus on security and identity. title: Possibilities for Potential DAOs
body:
There has been a lot of buzz around Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) in the last year. 

Any case in which people want greater ownership of the ways they live, work, and play could use a DAO to facilitate those activities. These cases often occur in the management of assets, facilitation of transactions, curation of products, and collaboration on work. 

Some specific areas that could benefit from DAO implementation in the future include:

- Philanthropy 
- Scientific funding
- Political groups
- News media 
- Social networks
- Real estate
- Housing markets 
- Sports 
- Casinos 
- Gaming 
- Insurance
- Research
- Supply chains
- Legal 
- Government 

There are innumerable possibilities for DAOs, both within and without these listed areas. **Here are some examples of current and potential types of DAOs.** 

*Philanthropic DAOs* 

Right now, when a donor gives money to a philanthropic cause, it usually travels through a long line of middlemen -  banks, lawyers, governments, and so on. Each of these steps takes away from the amount of money available to actually benefit the cause the donor originally sought to contribute to. 

With a charity DAO, these steps could be minimized and transparency could be maximized. A group already building a similar type of organization on the Ethereum platform is Humaniq. Their goal is to bring blockchain-based financial services to communities without access to banks (Davies). 

An important consideration when building a philanthropic DAO, however, is how to integrate ethics into the organization. If the community has full, unchecked control over where their funds are going, this might not always lead to the most socially responsible results. Using targeted governance strategies and some amount of planned centralization could solve that problem.

**pLIBRA Polkadot Bridge from LibraChina**

The pLibra project includes a bridge between Libra and Polkadot, a privacy-preserving Libra token, and a dApp ecosystem in Polkadot for Libra users. A cross-chain bridge is a way for networks to communicate, sending assets between chains. pLibra is made by LibraChina, a group dedicated to building applications on Libra. Co-founder Hang Yin took some time to answer my questions about project.

*What does LibraChina want users to know about the pLibra Polkadot bridge?*

pLibra is primarily a cross-chain bridge meant to allow for private transactions for Libra users, as well as opportunities for developers to build private dApps.

As Yin emphasized, pLibra, as an app with a token, is not a blockchain or even just a privacy token. Instead, it is the first application built on Phala Network, the smart contract blockchain at the core of LibraChina technology. According to Yin, Phala Network allows for a different kind of confidentiality than other privacy-focused blockchains.

While other confidential transaction chains use privacy coins, the goal of Phala Network is to secure privacy for all arbitrary information within smart contracts. The Phala white paper states that this is accomplished by introducing “an Event Sourcing / CQRS architecture into a [Trusted Execution Environment] TEE-blockchain hybrid system to archive cross-chain interoperability for the confidential smart contracts.”

Yin believes this allows for many more use cases, as Phala is meant to be a multi-purpose confidential platform.

## [How Can We Fix Tribalism in Cryptocurrency?](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/87)

At Berlin Blockchain Week '19, Commonwealth’s Chief-of-Staff Thom Ivy sat down with Gavin Wood for a chat on governance in the blockchain space. They started off talking about the importance of community response in handling toxic tribalism. In this piece, I take you into their conversation to show how a problem like tribalism could be solved with on-chain governance. 

“If community members are willing to publicly call out those who engage in personal attacks or aggressive tribalist behaviors, it can shift the culture and create new norms of conduct...By using on-chain governance to implement these kinds of changes, the community will be able to take full autonomy of their culture.”

## [Implementing Social Key Recovery](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/89)

Social Key Recovery lets your friends save a copy of your key, so that if you lose your key, your friends can help you out. But your friends don't just get a copy - they get a piece, or “shard,” of the key, and they have to work together to use it. 

If you shared your secret with three people, then you would need two of them to confirm your identity and deliver your secret back to you. The more shards you make and the more trusted contacts you introduce, the more secure your recovery key is. We explore the implementation options and consequences in this piece.

*"Right, and how do we un-fuck ourselves?”*  - Gian Volpicelli

### Day Two at Web3 Summit: The End of the Golden Age?

Day One of Web3 Summit 2019 wrapped up with Dr. Gavin Wood ruminating on the end of the Golden Age of Blockchain.

Dr. Wood believes that the openness and collaboration that has long been celebrated in the blockchain space is coming to an end, with competitive venture capitalism slowly invading the ecosystem. This certainly set the tone for Day Two of Web3 Summit, which focused much more on a need for privacy and independent software in the face of threatening state and corporate control.

### Snowden, Assange, and the Problem of Increasing Central Powers

Nearly every talk on the main stage during Day Two of the conference referenced oppressive central authority. Talks by Edward Snowden and from whistleblower advocate Naomi Colvin on the extradition of Julian Assange may have initially seemed slightly off-topic for the conference. However, Colvin was clear in her presentation defending WikiLeaks - the US government’s ongoing fight to extradite Assange symbolizes the power of the state to crush anyone who acts against the will of those people in power. Colvin emphasized that the language used in legal materials for the case would set a precedent for the US to have power over anyone they deem even tangentially related to facilitating those disapproved acts. 

Especially in a space where freedom is so highly valued, those creating technology for a decentralized Internet should not allow themselves to be threatened simply for producing a platform that gives people more autonomy. This was Colvin’s main, haunting message to the audience: there is a need to stand up against encroaching power now, before it gets any further and truly can smother the blockchain space.

title: A Reputation Bridge for Pseudonymous Identities
body:
### Assume a Spherical Cow

Or, instead, assume a crypto-Twitter. That’s the future platform angel investor Balaji Srinivasan envisioned when explaining how pseudonymous identities could be linked to reputation, without losing anonymity. 

In the world we live in now, even when an online identity is pseudonymous for the purpose of being anonymous, there are ways to track activity and see patterns in a way that makes it possible to clearly identify the person behind the pseudonym. This becomes a problem when you need to be truly anonymous, but you also need to interact with others online in a way that lets you use the weight of your reputation. 

This is where Srinivasan’s future crypto-Twitter comes in. In this example, reputation is quantified in followers. Obviously, if you created a pseudonym and transferred all of your public followers to it, it wouldn’t be very anonymous. Yet, you need followers to give you reputational weight. 

Srinivasan’s answer to this issue is twofold. First, the crypto-Twitter would need a back end that would allow for a zero-knowledge transfer of followers. A zero-knowledge (ZK) proof is a tool that allows you to prove that some information is true, without revealing the contents of that information. In this example, the ZK proof would conclusively tell the Twitter operator that you have, say, 1,000 followers, but it wouldn’t reveal any information about who those followers are. In this way, the system could verify your pseudonym, proving that you have a reputation without ever knowing the details behind that reputation. 

While this verification shouldn’t reveal the pseudonym’s true identity, it still reveals some information. Thus comes the second part of Srinivasan’s solution: an “auto-follow” system. title: Diverse Structures and Challenges for Oracles
body:
### What is an oracle in the blockchain world?

Oracles are the truth-giving tools that send data to and from smart contracts to allow for proper execution. For instance, imagine Alice participates in a smart contract that says that Bob will send a certain amount of money to her if she sends Bob an email. The smart contract would have all the information necessary to send Alice the money once the email is received by Bob. But once the contract is deployed, it can’t be edited and has no way to find information about whether or not Bob received his present. 

This is where an oracle comes in. The oracle’s job is to find out whether or not Bob actually received the email. As soon as the oracle confirms that Bob received Alice’s email, it sends that information to the smart contract. The smart contract is assured that the parameters were filled, and it executes the final task of sending Alice her money. 

Oracles can either be software or hardware oracles, and they can be inbound or outbound. The names are pretty indicative of their qualities, but with technology as new and significant as oracles, we might as well start with some definitions. Software oracles are meant to collect information available online, while hardware oracles collect data from hardware located and collecting info in the physical world. Meanwhile, inbound oracles provide external information to the smart contract and outbound oracles allow smart contracts to send information out (Voshmgir).

### What are the challenges for developing oracles?

There are three ways to structure an oracle:
- Integrated within a protocol, coded by and for that particular chain.
- Centralized, using a trusted third party to supply information.
- Decentralized, using a network of oracle nodes.

The main argument against an integrated oracle is that it is inefficient in terms of both time and cost (Chainlink). Moreover, a centralized oracle has all the drawbacks that anything centralized does: it requires a lot of trust

title: Outlook on Blockchain and Quantum Computing
body:
Ideas about the implications of quantum computing for cryptography have been circulating for a while, with opinions generally ranging from “it will have no effect” to “we’re doomed.” Regardless of your stance, it’s important to at least consider a future in which this technology will significantly alter our infrastructure. 

### The Rapid Development of Quantum Processing Power

In order to build an understanding of what quantum computers will mean for the world of blockchain, we’ll start with some basic definitions. Right now, everyday computers use bits - binary pieces of computing power that scale linearly. The pieces of computing power used by quantum computers, qubits, are able to represent both zeros and ones at once and thus scale exponentially. This means that every qubit added to a system doubles its computation power. 

In 2015, computers were developed that used 4 qubits. By 2018, Intel had created a 49-qubit processor, and Google had made a 72-qubit system (Matier). Just yesterday, Google officially announced that its quantum machine achieved “quantum supremacy,” meaning that their computer was able to complete a calculation that even the best classical computer could not complete (at least not within a time frame of fewer than 10,000 years) (Arute et al.). 

Quantum computers are clearly developing at a very fast pace. Will the extraordinary power of quantum computers mean the end of cryptographic security? 

### Quantum Implications for Blockchain

The extreme power behind quantum computers has obvious implications for blockchains that use Proof-of-Work. Because miners using classical computers are the ones securing the chain, the introduction of a more powerful computer could be detrimental to the safety of a PoW network. For example, there has been speculation that the Grover algorithm, which allows for quadratic speed up in searches, could be used to break a hashing function like SHA-256 (this is the technology Bitcoin is based on). title: Sustaining Open Source Funding
body:
Dr. Gavin Wood recently explained why he thinks we are in the last phases of a so-called “Golden Age of Blockchain.” In his view, open-source development has been celebrated in the space for a long time, but we’re about to see the end of that. According to Dr. Wood, with increased competition, collaboration and openness will be replaced by competitive attitudes and profit-seeking motivations. 

Despite this pessimistic tone, there are still many who are working to encourage, sustain, and scale opportunities for open-source software. Dries Buytaert, one of the minds behind Drupal, has outlined some clear challenges and possibilities he sees for scaling open source projects.

### Recommendations for Sustaining Open-Source

Buytaert defines people engaged with open source projects as either Makers, those who develop out of and contribute back to open-source software, or Takers, those who monetize open source projects without giving back. Obviously, a significant part of scalability is sustainability. Open-source software will not be continually developed if end users are mostly Takers. 

In understanding how to solve this problem, Buytaert first explains the separation of common and public goods. Common goods are defined as rivalrous, or those that diminish with use, while public goods are non-rivalrous, a never-ending resource. Open-source software is a public good, but for companies that answer to corporate sponsors, customers are a common good. Therefore, it is necessary to develop governance mechanisms for open source software that encourage software free-riders but discourages customer free-riders (Buytaert).  

Buytaert describes the three ways this problem is usually dealt with as self-governance, centralization (central maintenance) or privatization (maintenance in exchange for exclusive benefits).

title: The State of Over-the-Counter Crypto Trading
body:
### What is OTC trading?

Over-the-Counter (OTC) trading is trading of securities that do not appear on a formal securities exchange. While exchanges are limited in liquidity to the individuals participating in the market and the liquidity of each currency involved at any point in time, OTC markets are meant to present an opportunity for more liquidity, as well as better communication and privacy (Dale). Closely related to the term OTC is the idea of a Decentralized Exchange (DEX), an exchange for which there is no supervisory authority.

Traditionally, items like American depository receipts (ADRs) (which represent stock that is traded on a foreign exchange), bank bonds, or derivatives have been traded on OTC markets. The entities trading in these markets have often been smaller companies that don’t meet the requirements to be listed in an official exchange, or that want to avoid associated fees. There is a risk in not having a supervisory exchange, but also more freedom and potential for reward - which is perhaps why larger companies, like Chinese multi-media giant Tencent or Nestle, the largest food company in the world, also trade on OTC markets (Murphy). 

### What does OTC look like for cryptocurrency trading?

There are quite a few cryptocurrency OTC desks, including Cumberland, Jump, and Circle. Moreover, bigger cryptocurrency exchanges are increasingly offering their own OTC platforms. Many of these exchange-related OTC desks have a very high entrance thresh hold, though. For example, a recently published Coin Telegraph article by Elijah Bradley notes that the Binance OTC desk will only facilitate transactions higher than 20 BTC ($69,552), and the Bittrex desk only supports trade commitments of $250,000 or more. 

This push to offer OTC market platforms is probably due to the fact that OTC is wildly popular among the crypto community. In April 2018, the OTC market handled between $250 million and $30 billion in trades every day, while exchanges managed just

title: Diversifying Delegations & Stake Distribution: The Cosmos Example
body:
### Cosmos Stake Distribution and Validator Centralization

On September 5, 2019, Felix Lutsch of Chorus One took a snapshot of Cosmos Hub token holder and validator data in order to analyze the stake distribution in one of the first live Proof-of-Stake networks. Lutsch found some curious results, the most prominent of which was a lack of validator diversification on the network. 

Lutsch used the Stargazer API to analyze active delegations, as well as the corresponding size and validator addresses. An important caveat is that addresses are not necessarily one entity - the analysis was not able to account for whether or not one entity held multiple holder addresses.

At the time data was collected, the researcher saw “11,387 active delegations from 6,459 addresses on the Cosmos Hub.” Lutsch cites the average address as having 1.76 active delegations, which means very little diversification among delegators to different validators. 

Lutsch also noted that the top three most delegated-to validators s charge little-to-no  commission fee. The top validators by number of delegations and by amount of stake either fall into the less than 5% commission fee range, or greater than 10%. There are very few mid-range commission fee validators in the top 15% of validators. 

Validators that charge a very low fee are extremely popular among smaller holders, which makes a lot of sense. There are some curious outliers, though. For instance, Cosmostation, which is ranked at 7 in terms of amount of stake, has a validator fee of 12%, but also has one of the highest amounts of delegators, at 678. Lutsch surmised that it could be their high-quality wallet that brings so many delegators with relatively small holdings to the validator, even with the high fee.

title: The Argument for Blockchain-based Privacy
body:
A big driver behind all blockchain development is the dual promise of transparency and privacy. A blockchain, after all, is a ledger meant to permanently describe all interactions that occur on the chain network. What sort of transparency that description should offer is open to experimentation, but there is widespread agreement that blockchain transactions should be as anonymous as possible. 

### What is the best way to do privacy?

General practices for anonymity include using pseudonymous identities, finding ways to create a verifiable and un-forge-able signature, and securely storing transaction data. There are a few ways to implement these privacy strategies. Mixing services are a prominent example. Traditional mixers have been implemented to tumble coins from transactions together, making it impossible to trace who the original payer of a coin was (Clifford). Meanwhile, a mixnet like that proposed first by David Chaum and implemented recently by NYM technologies routes transaction data through several nodes, which each mix and bounce multiple transaction datasets (Web3 Foundation). This makes it nearly impossible to determine where transactions were coming and going to. 

A variation on the mixing idea called ring signatures applies the scrambling idea to digital signatures. The mechanism groups together signers and only reveals that the signature comes from the group, not which member of the group it was made by. Another way of obfuscating identity is the generation of one-time-use, randomly produced “stealth addresses” (Clifford).

Homomorphic encryption, on the other hand, uses an algebraic system to allow data to be processed and operated on without revealing any information about the data (Crane). Zero-Knowledge Succinct ARguments of Knowledge, or zk-SNARKs, can be used for a similar purpose: proving a fact about something, without actually revealing the information that proves that fact. body:
### Big Roadblocks for Telegram Open Network 

Telegram Open Network (TON) has had a tumultuous month. On October 11th, the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filed an emergency restraining order to stop the network from releasing it tokens to initial investors, declaring that the initial coin sale (which hit $1.7 million) was illegal. On October 12th, the TON Telegram Channel saw all messages from board members deleted and the announcement of an immediate, temporary hold on development (Partz). 

When TON originally commenced their token sale, investors were told that they would receive their money back if the network did not launch on the promised date of October 31, 2019. Since the SEC injunction, the initial investors have agreed to allow the launch date to be shifted to April 30, 2020. An SEC hearing that was scheduled for October 24th has also been moved to February 2020, with Telegram describing the shift positively. However, investors are not all so positive. According to a Coindesk interview with an anonymous investor, the source believes that TON will not be able to settle with the SEC, and the network will eventually lose the US as a market, as well as other huge communities in China, Russia, and around Europe (Foxley). 

According to Coin Telegraph, the SEC’s issue is with the way Telegram filed for the right to sell a security. In February of 2019, Telegram filed with the SEC for this right and received approval, but with the caveat that the security token can only be sold to accredited initial investors. Despite the fact that the initial coin sale was made to accredited investors, the SEC believes that the coins will easily be sold to other, non-accredited investors, which they argue puts Telegram in violation of their regulations (Linver).
