title: Why Isn't Blockchain Part of the Real World?
body:
Earlier this month, Laura Shin published a podcast titled “Althea Network: How Ethereum Is Used in the Real World.” The episode covers how the Althea network is serving as a decentralized Internet provider, allowing neighbors to support community Internet access using pay-as-you-go stablecoin plans (Shin). While Althea is an innovative alternative to traditional ISPs, the title of the podcast episode reveals an interesting disconnect in the blockchain ecosystem: the idea that blockchain technology exists separately from the “real world.”

### The Adoption Problem

This attitude largely stems from the lack of adoption of blockchain technology by what is sometimes labeled the “traditional” world. This points to a problem that many in the blockchain space have identified and are fighting against: the high barrier to the ecosystem given the level of technical knowledge needed to build and use blockchain-based technologies. As Aidan Hyman elucidated at Web3 Summit 2019, "If we want real people building real stuff, we need to abstract this technology to a place where not just subject matter experts are building, but people are building this for the world, for themselves" (Web3 Foundation). 

This problem is not new. In fact, David Chaum faced the same problem when he first introduced cryptocurrency in the form of eCash in the 1990s. “It was hard to get enough merchants to accept it, so that you could get enough consumers to use it, or vice versa,” Chaum told Forbes in 1999, after DigiCash had finally filed for bankruptcy. “As the Web grew, the average level of sophistication of users dropped. It was hard to explain the importance of privacy to them” (Wirdum).

title: The Evolution of Web3 Wallets
body:
### Takeaways

- Crypto wallets have developed beyond a bare-bones tool for sending and receiving money, to mechanisms that optimize the experience of using the blockchain-based currency, organizations, and applications that make up the Web 3.0 ecosystem
- As DAOs and dApps evolve, wallets have been and will continue evolving with them. There are currently some challenges to adopting these Web 3.0 wallets, however, including troublesome login processes and trade-offs between security and ease-of-use 
- Smart contract wallets that are vulnerable to bugs but secure their funds with a protocol-based insurance platform like Nexus Mutual are a prime example of some of the current challenges and innovation in the Web 3.0 wallet game

### Wallets in the Blockchain Ecosystem 

Wallets are crucial for interacting with blockchains - and right now, as blockchain-based technologies are rapidly evolving, so is the wallet ecosystem. Check out my closer look at the recent article, “An Overview of the Crypto Wallet Landscape,” from 1confirmation’s Richard Chen.  

### A Brief History of Crypto Wallets 

Chen begins his account by describing some of the first digital wallets. These were initially created in a way that was very transparent about the cryptography beneath the surface: the existence of private and public keys. Early on, the method was to write down your mnemonic, or seed phase, that locked the wallet - but that’s not very secure, and it’s not reasonable to ask people to memorize a random grouping of words and numbers. Projects like BrainWallet evolved to let people choose their own seed phrases, but perhaps as expected, people are too predictable and hackers early on were able to steal millions of dollars worth of Bitcoins (Chen).

title: Leveraging Reputation with Blockchain
body:
## Takeaways

- Reputation is a powerful tool, and how to use it in blockchain technology is just beginning to be explored
- Some blockchain tech that leverages reputation includes Token Curated Registries, Reputation Curated Registries, Pseudonymous Reputation Bridges, and Reputation-Based Voting
- While there is good reason to be cautious, we should continue experimenting with how the powerful tool of reputation could be used to optimize human organization, governance, and development practices. 

### How to Use Reputation on Blockchains 

Reputation is powerful - and blockchain-based technology gives us unique new ways to explore how we might leverage that power to design better organizational structures. That’s a broad area, though, and one that has only seen early exploration efforts to far. So what are the intersection points of blockchain and reputation right now?

**Token Curated Registry (TCR)**

The idea for a Token Curated Registry is to use crypto-economic incentives to build a list that leverages a community’s collective knowledge in order to build a good list. Token Curated Registries were initially introduced by Mike Gouldin, working on adChain Registry, a TCR in which token holders verify that domain names are not fraudulent (Token Curated Registry). 

The list curated through a Token Curated Registry could be anything, blockchain-related or not - from best restaurants in Detroit to most reliable validators. TCRs could each have their own native currency and compete to attract the most and the best data, as well as the most skilled knowledge-builders. 

You could buy a token, put stake with your application to add something to the list. If someone challenges your application, it can be put to a vote. body:
## Takeaways

- The Tezos Babylon Upgrade, implemented on October 18, 2019, marked the first time a protocol has successfully automatically implemented two upgrades, and the first time two independent developer teams worked together to implement a proposal.
- Notable changes include introducing quorum caps, a new consensus algorithm, and changes to the coding language that allow for improved smart contract interactions
- Developers of the upgrade have reflected that increased documentation, more time for community testing and feedback, and a faster voting period could have facilitated a better upgrade process

-----

### A First for On-chain Governance: the 2nd Update to the Tezos Protocol

The Babylon Upgrade, implemented on October 18, 2019, was the second amendment to the Tezos protocol via the Tezos governance mechanism. The upgrade marked the first time a protocol has successfully automatically implemented two upgrades, which were approved by the community and initiated with the governance system (Tezos Foundation). 

The Babylon Upgrade was developed by TQ Tezos, Nomadic Labs, and Cryptium Labs (Tezos Foundation). According to a post from Cryptium Labs’ founder Awa Sun Yin, the upgrade, which is also known as protocol 005 and was successfully activated on block 655361, marks another first: the first time two independent developer teams worked together to implement a proposal. 

### Babylon's Changes

Cryptium Labs lists the following successful changes under the Babylon Upgrade: 

- Addition of quorum caps
- Transition to Emmy+
- Making implicit accounts delegatable
- Implementing multiple big_maps and entrypoints
- Adding spam prevention for proposals (Yin)

Quorum caps will be at 20 and 70 percent, in order to ensure enough participation, but also hopefully avoid capture of votes by any entity (McKenzie).

body:
Will we understand that code is law and leverage that knowledge to embed the values we want to see in the structure of the Internet? This is the question Lawrence Lessig asked in his essay from the year 2000, [*Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace*](https://harvardmagazine.com/2000/01/code-is-law-html). Lessig, the respected academic and political activist who once served as the director of the Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics at Harvard University, actually coined the term “code is law.” At the turn of the century, Lessig elucidated the way code regulates how life on the Internet can be lived by limiting access, privacy, and individual control. And whether it is traditional governments and commerce systems or simply coders, someone has the power to determine how code is used to regulate freedom. In the author’s words, “Unless we understand how cyberspace can embed, or displace, values from our constitutional tradition, we will lose control over those values.”

Lessig first explained the regulatory nature of code in his 1999 book *Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace*, but if you don’t have time for that read, his essay linked above is certainly worth a read. In it, Lessig alludes to the foundational issues we are still struggling with today in the blockchain-based, Web 3.0 ecosystem: the challenges of designing liberty-preserving Internet architectures, avoiding system capture by partial interests, and implementing self-governance.

title: Burnt Oak: Bootstrapping Edgeware community
body:
## Introduction

The mainnet launch has been disappointing in light of the successful Lockdrop campaign. The complexity, instability and novel character of the Substrate tech stack has been underestimated. Consequently a rather active community with high expectations went into hibernation mode (waiting for a relaunch). 

We propose to test and fix bugs under an incentivized regime before mainnet launch codenamed Burnt Oak.

[https://commonwealth-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/47ec08bf-a31d-4d77-9ee1-fad40b2b3227.png]

The goal of Burnt Oak is a wider ownership distribution according to one’s contribution. 

Bleeding-edge technology requires certain effort in terms of testing. Burnt Oak invites  a wide set of individuals to test  for the rich set of different setups and combinations before the production phase.

This approach is inspired by the so called [Game of Stakes](https://medium.com/coinmonks/breaking-down-the-cosmos-game-of-stakes-5cbc538bcedb) - incentivized testnet period before launch of Cosmos network, an approach followed by other PoS protocols. 

As there is no concrete plan for allotment of outstanding 2.5% EDG tokens from genesis allocation (whitepaper states that these funds should be used as a reward for testnet/early participants and early contributors outlined also [here](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/48) and [here](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/49) ), we propose that the community defines concrete rules and mechanics for their distribution, laying the foundation for an ongoing bug bounty program, funding of Edgeware development etc..

title: How do stablecoins work and should we use them?
body:
## Takeaways 

- Stablecoins can be tied to fiat currency in a bank, cryptocurrency collateral, or supported by an algorithmic “central bank.” Each method has pros and cons, with trust problems ranging from dependence on an over-centralized issuer to reliance on an experimental algorithm.
- Stablecoins are often thought of as a type of cryptocurrency that is compliant or familiar enough to traditional financial norms to see mass adoption. However, many coins don’t actually embrace the dual promise of transparency and privacy that blockchain offers.
- Recent criticism of Tether’s lack of transparency and the possibility that their dishonest minting strategy led to serious market manipulation and the 2017 Bitcoin boom demonstrates some of the major problems with stablecoins. 

### What are stablecoins and why should we care?

Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies that are tied (or pegged, or tethered) to another kind of asset. The coins are named “stable” because they are designed to sit right in that sweet spot between crypto market volatility and fiat money unreliability. 

The stablecoin market is big - last February, the market value was at $3 billion, twice the size it was a year previously. They’ve gotten a lot of attention recently in the global sphere because Libra is meant to be a stablecoin, tethered to a big basket of other assets. But questions about transparency and trust for stablecoin issuers have led to questions about whether stablecoins do any good for the wider crypto ecosystem - or if they should even be considered part of the ecosystem in the first place.

### How do stablecoins work?

There are three popular stablecoin models for tethering a coin to another asset, including:

- Backing the stablecoin with fiat currency in a bank.
- Backing the stablecoin with cryptocurrency collateral.
- Backing the stablecoin with a “central bank” defined by algorithms (Orcutt).

Each of these methods has its own pros and cons. While backing the stablecoin with cash

title: Using an Iterative Comparison Algorithm to Rank Abstract Value
body:
## Takeaways

- Iterative Comparison Algorithms face the problem of ranking abstract value by judging value based on a comparison, rather than trying to quantify an abstract worth. 
- There is an obvious challenge to this model: the set of people using the ICA to make the ranked list could be implicitly biased, or explicitly collude to manipulate the outcome. 
- Could established techniques for decentralization and anti-collusion be applied to the ICA to ensure its success? Would a holographic consensus-like auditing layer work? 

### How can we rank something with abstract values? 

I want to share an alternative to [quantifying reputation as a way to judge value](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/129-leveraging-reputation-with-blockchain). Instead, I want to examine an Iterative Comparison Algorithm - an algorithm that decides the value of something based on its comparative value, as introduced by Cent.

The clearest blocker to implementing reputation in formal systems is that reputation is inherently abstract. This is the same issue that Kevin Owocki brings up as a [challenge for funding open-source development](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/116) - that it’s not possible to accurately judge how much a developer should be awarded for their work because the value of the work is inherently abstract. This problem of judging abstract value comes up in a lot of places, and Iterative Comparison Algorithms face it by not quantifying value, but instead building a ranking based on a comparison. 

The ICA would give you a choice between two things, and have you choose which is better. This is much easier than trying to assign an arbitrary number or to choose a limited set of parameters to judge value on. And if you were able to get enough people to answer the survey, you would get a reasonably “objective” answer.

title: A quick update leading up to mainnet launch
body:
At this point we're still waiting on a few major fixes to launch a stable Edgeware testnet.

**Online validator slashing issue**: We've observed a slashing issue where at times batches of 'im_online' heartbeats will not be registered by the chain. This causes large numbers of well-behaving validators to be slashed for being offline. This doesn't appear to have happened on Kusama CC2/PoS, so we think the problem will be resolved shortly, either by our forthcoming upgrade to the latest Substrate master, or by further debugging.

**Storage root mismatch issue**: There is a node crash that happens occasionally. The underlying cause is that the trie storage root may get out of sync. This happens infrequently enough that it's difficult to debug, but a tentative fix is in the works. In the interim, node operators should run node management software which monitors for the Edgeware process going down and restarts it when necessary.

The forthcoming testnet, which will probably be versioned 0.10, will provide the all-clear for mainnet launch ideally at the end of this month.

In the meantime, we're continuing to make improvements to the Commonwealth interface. Around the end of this month, we'll have a much user-friendlier interface for composing new discussions and comments, and a new and improved design for user profiles. Later this year we'll introduce integrations with other platforms like Github, Discord, Discourse, and Riot, so you can keep track of all the progress happening on Edgeware starting from one place.

title: Organizational Governance Mechanisms for Blockchains
body:
## Takeaways

- Blockchains today represent the ultimate meeting of cryptography and decentralized human networks, and how to best integrate organizational governance mechanisms into those systems is just beginning to be truly explored.  
- Network governance mechanisms must look different for different types of blockchains. There can be variations in how voting happens, how treasury funds are raised and used, dispute resolution processes, oracle structures, as well as levels of decentralization and off-chain engagement.
- Governance choices are made at different levels of chain infrastructure. At every layer, crypto-economic primitives, concepts of game theory, and alignment on principals and incentives are key for designing good governance structures. 
- **Are there any community governance mechanisms you’re passionate about?** Any unforeseen challenges that people should pay more attention to?

### Why is governance important for blockchains?

Governance is a hugely important topic in the crypto world. Because blockchains today represent the ultimate meeting of cryptography and decentralized human networks, how to best integrate management controls into those systems is a question full of exciting possibilities that are just beginning to be truly explored (de Filippi & McMullen). It’s too soon to know what governance structures are the most effective; even at a primitive level, it’s unclear what type of governance mechanisms work best for what cases.

title: Foundational Text: The Social Smart Contract
body:
Anybody looking for concrete examples of the current intersections of cutting-edge blockchain technology research and socio-political structures should take a peek at [“The Social Smart Contract”](https://github.com/DemocracyEarth/paper#ii_Contents) from Democracy Earth.

Democracy Earth is a group working to enabled token-based, open community participation. “The Social Smart Contract” is a three-part document with a manifesto for idealists, a paper for builders, and execution instructions for the pragmatists. In the authors’ words, their goal is for the document to be “a living roadmap for planetary governance.” Given the importance of the Internet in modern-day politics, Democracy Earth hopes “to continue paving the road of implementations that enable cryptographic open-audit voting.”

While using blockchain for voting isn’t exactly novel, the actual proposal is innovative in its breadth and depth of research. The manifesto is particularly interesting, diving into fundamental topics from network theory and globalization to modern geopolitics and AI governance. The paper itself elucidates how liquid democracy, Ethereum’s Solidity smart contracts, segregated witness, and the Lightning Protocol can be used to implement a democracy that provides everything from self-sovereign identity to Universal Basic Income.

Definitely an essential read for those interested in applied blockchain governance innovations and the intersection of blockchain and politics.

title: Tests and Opportunities for Curation Markets
body:
## Takeaways

- Curation Markets, originally introduced by Simon de la Rouviere, are meant to allow markets to coordinate on a goal or topic. A token associated with the market can be used to meaningfully evaluate the value and the curation of the goal or topic.
- The token would also have a continuous pricing model according to a bonding curve. As more people buy tokens and the number of tokens increases, the price to get a token also increases.
- Design challenges include a bonding curve potentially disadvantaging participants who are less able to put stake in the market early on, and the possibility for people to enter the market who are not incentivized to curate honestly. 
- Intentional token bonding curve design and good governance are necessary to face these challenges, though the concept is still too experimental to have defined standards.

### What is a Curation Market?

Curation Markets, originally introduced by Simon de la Rouviere, are meant to allow markets to coordinate on a goal or topic with value. This goal or topic can be anything from a meme (by its original definition, a unit of cultural value), to a trait you want to see in your community. Each curation market is formed around one of these specific ideas, and a token associated with the market can be used to meaningfully evaluate the value and the curation of the goal or topic (Token Engineering).

It all sounds a bit abstract, so I’ll give an example that de la Rouviere recently explained on an Epicenter podcast. Let’s say Cape Town, South Africa, was experiencing a drought (as it has recently), and conserving water became a desirable trait, or a goal for the town. You could create a curation market around saving water. Restaurants that save water could buy “water conservation” tokens, which would let them receive more business as more people around town see that they have this desirable trait. title: Edgeware Communications Strategy - Update
body:
## Edgeware Communications Strategy - Update 

I had a very interesting call today with [Joon Ian Wong](https://twitter.com/joonian) who is a well respected journalist in the space. His background spans technology and business reporting at Quartz, media startups in Asia, and he was early at Coindesk, launching their Consensus event. He is also one of the founders of the [ACJR](https://acjr.network/) (Association of Crypto Journalists & Researchers) whose Telegram group contains the great and the good of crypto-reporters.

Aside from this he is also deep into the world of Personal / Social / Community Tokens and has been experimenting there as one of the founders of [Seed Club](https://seedclub.xyz/) so he has a very hands on approach.

**Why the discussion was timely **
We are currently finalising the recruitment of [a project PR agency ](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/859-edgeware-comms-strategy-discussion-document)and one of the things we need to balance carefully is how we as a community project balance funding of 'PR' and the funding of 'independent media DAOs' that are born from the chain.

In effect, how do we draw a line between more explicit 'marketing and PR' and the funding of public goods? 

Currently there is no clear definition as to how we separate the two, and it is a distinction that needs to be made - or at least discussed. 

**The independent media challenge **
Traditionally in newsrooms there has always been a clear dividing line between editorial and commercial imperatives, to ensure reporting remains balanced and independent - akin to the separation of church and state. 

In the last few decades, the rise of 24/7 news, digital media networks, branded content and social media that are all the products of advertising models that prioritise attention have seen this dividing line eaten away, leading to an erosion in trust as profits trump purpose and everything becomes about clicks.

[POAP](https://www.poap.xyz/) is Proof of Attendance Protocol that was built on Ethereum but now is running on xDai chain (because of high gas fees for token transfers, transaction costs). POAPs were being used on physical events where organisers were giving them away to attendees and people then could either compare their NFTs or just use as an ice breaker for talking about Ethereum conferences that they visited. As event has flipped into virtual space the POAP craze is still going on strongly. Another usability of these tokens that I find very interesting is that POAP NFT holders are allowed to take apart in governance process and vote on proposals see [https://poap.vote/](https://poap.vote/).

title: Signing legal agreements
body:
Smart contracts gain even more possibilities when they are merged with legal contracts. 
Hybrid contracts consist of both  distributed code and legalese. One example might be the start of a new venture with its own LLC and tokens. The smart contract address for the tokens, and the signed operating agreement, would together make a hybrid contract. 
As part of the LexBridge proposal, Commonwealth users will be able to issue and sign legal agreements; opening up the ecosystem to hybrid contracts.

The initial milestone will cover signing documents as an individual through the Polkadot browser extension. 
Most of this process is already sketched out: a PDF is generated clientside, and the hash of this is signed and stashed on a distributed ledger as proof of signing.  

I am seeking insight on how we might best sign statements using Edgeware; for both individuals and as groups. 

Following signing by individual accounts,  support for multisig wallets and DAOs to sign legal contracts will be the focus of the LexBridge proposal. Most multisig and DAO implementations support signing of statements or signaling votes; sufficient for legal agreements. 

Eventually, though, there will need to be some process by which smart and legal contracts, once signed,  kick off further events; from AWS to Ethereum to Edgeware, opening up a cascade of possibilities. Polkadot supports this bridge, in theory, but it will take the entire community to build it.

title: Verifying ERUP 3.0 "Tokyo"
body:
This is the list of steps I took to verify the proposed "ERUP 3.0" upgrade, named "Tokyo", specifically the "v45" runtime. 

## Verify WASM Binary

First thing I did is check is that the generated WASM checksum of the project matches the uploaded binary.

I did this by checking out the repo at the `v3.2.0` tag and following the `srtool` command line items here, then verifying the content and SHA256 match exactly: [https://github.com/hicommonwealth/edgeware-node/releases/tag/v3.2.0](https://github.com/hicommonwealth/edgeware-node/releases/tag/v3.2.0)

## Attempt "No-op" Dev Upgrade

Next thing to check is that upgrading on an already-up-to-date node has no effect.

1. First ensure that the `srtool` step ran successfully, so you have a generated wasm file at `./target/srtool/release/wbuild/edgeware-runtime/edgeware_runtime.compact.wasm`
2. Then, build the node itself using the setup script `./setup.sh`.
3. Run a development node: `./target/release/edgeware --dev --tmp`
4. Attach to the development node on [https://polkadot.js.org/apps/](https://polkadot.js.org/apps/) by selecting "Local Node" in the sidebar and hitting "Switch". Page should refresh.
5. Attempt an upgrade by going to "Developer → Sudo", hitting "File Upload" on the code input and selecting the built wasm from step 1, and checking "With Weight Override" and setting it to "1". Then hit "Submit Sudo Unchecked". A modal should pop up, showing "Alice" as the account. Hit "Sign and Submit". Eventually the notifications on the top-right should show an extrinsic success.
6. Verify that the chain is still producing blocks, refresh the page and ensure balances etc. are all as expected — nothing should have happened, because I upgraded the runtime to itself.

## Attempt Dev Upgrade

Next I ran a "real" upgrade on a v3.1.0 development node.

2. Clone a new copy of `edgeware-node` and check out `v3.1.0`.

title: Verifying the Tokyo runtime proposal
body:
# Overview
Last week or so I proposed the Tokyo upgrade release to the Edgeware democracy / council as an external proposal. There have been a few members of Commonwealth who have tested the release and some have added that they had issues replicating the release's hash on chain. This post is my process for handling the release.

# Srtool
It seems we can all replicate the `srtool` output using chevdor's script. First, I would recommend checking out the release:
cd edgeware-node
git checkout v3.2.0
Then, run the scripts needed to instantiate `srtool`. You will need docker in order to make this part work. For more information about `srtool` please refer to https://www.chevdor.com/project/2020/2020-srtool/.
export RUSTC_VERSION=nightly-2020-07-20; export PACKAGE=edgeware-runtime; alias srtool='docker run --rm -it -e PACKAGE=$PACKAGE -v $PWD:/build -v /tmp/cargo:/cargo-home chevdor/srtool:$RUSTC_VERSION'

srtool build edgeware-runtime

There has been consistent community interest in finding additional venues for liquidity for Edgeware. Exchange C, a top 15 exchange by normalized volume by Coingecko has approached us about advancing a community proposal for exchange listing.

Like previous proposals for [Exchange A](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/827-proposal-top-15-exchange-by-cmc-integration-exchange-a) and [Exchange B](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/1004-proposal-exchange-b-edg), There are two components to this proposal:

## Proposal Pt 1.
**Exchange Integration and Marketing Cost**

The exchange has asked for an amount of EDG that covers:

1. Integration Fee (half in EDG and half in a stablecoin)
2. Marketing Campaign funds, to be distributed in a marketing campaign


Like previous proposals, while the fee is relatively straightforward, we’ve been asked to keep the exact amount confidential. Naturally, this makes a community vote difficult. To balance the dual need for confidentiality and transparency, a treasury proposal will ask for a “buffer” amount of EDG that is between **1.2x - 1.7x** the integration and marketing campaign.

This buffer amount will be allocated to 2-of-3 multsig, where only one member of the multisig is on the Commonwealth team. This should allow for a third party to monitor any transaction between the multisig and the exchange.

From here, the full amount will be deposited into the exchange. While the integration and marketing will be allocated to the exchange, the remainder of the buffer could be used for market making. After a set amount of time of at least 6 months, the buffer amount would be able to be returned to the Edgeware Treasury.

Following on from the successful PR & Communications vote, I have had our first call with Market Across. 
I hoped this would be a call to launch the project, however, there are some things outstanding:

- Market Across were not aware of our chosen package

- Internally we will need to decide what exactly we would like to push. My recommendation is the initial months should be dedicated to growing awareness for Edgeware in an attempt to onboard quality projects.

- Plan - Who, What, Where, When, Why. We will need to effectively communicate this with MA and set clear progression goals in our communications.

title: Multiple Edgeware Chains: What does that look like?
body:
This post is mostly to inspire and explore the near-medium term future of how chains are developing and how we may grow in response using a multi-chain ecosystem architecture.


Currently we have 1 chain, Edgeware, and a testnet.  Ethereum maintains a few testnets for different reasons, and a mature Edgeware would likely do the same, one being the codename Hedgeware chain that would help test parachain bonding in a value-bearing way; the 'canary net' model. 

We're also seeing multi-chain architectures e.g. Binance, with a split between Binance Chain and Binance Smart Chain, where each uses the other for specific purposes.

Binance:
- Focused on solely transactions, orderbook matching, asset exchange. 


Binance Smart Chain
- More EVM, user-uploaded logic execution and contracts broadly. 


Use cases will increasingly require unique technical operations - derivatives for instance require high compute and high TPS. 

Legal and jurisdictional requirements may also increasingly hold on how chains develop, for instance, whether KYC is required, or the reverse- where we want all chain interactions to be utterly ZK private.

Additionally, we've seen a set of chains devoted to other use cases like NFTs (Flow) and Gaming (Enjin.)

So with that said, there is a potential future where there is a 'family' of Edgeware chains each purposed for specific needs, but with a trusted relationship between one another (bridges,) or Edgeware Relay Chain uniting this set. They would all use the same Token, (EDG) 

## Example:
(DOT) Polkadot Network
>
(EDG) Edgeware Parachain Slot (Either acting as Edgeware Relay also or serving as a proxy, but depending on how swappable consensus plays out, we can imagine that seperating these roles might be useful.)
>
(EDG)  **Edgeware Relay** (Our current Mainchain could do this, as it maintains our val community!) 
- Edgeware EVM
- Edgeware Complex Defi
- Edgeware KYC-Ready
- Edgeware ZK Total Privacy
- Edgeware Wasm
- Edgeware NFTs
- Edgeware Canaryne

title: Keeping up with Kulupu
body:
Kulupu's going to have a baby! It's called [Neatcoin](https://neatcoin.org/) and it 'll be a PoS chain supporting a variant of Diem's (former Facebook's Libra) smart contract language Move called Outmove. It will also bring Grin's Mimblewimble privacy transactions to Substrate.

Kulupu holders will be able to get $Neat via a lockdrop. A cool feature is that holders can repeatedly lock their already locked coins for potential new drops and also use them for governance.

To enable trading between both coins the[ atomic swap](https://github.com/paritytech/substrate/tree/master/frame/atomic-swap) pallet will be integrated. [@drewstone](/edgeware/account/hwR8hAatmmdupBLXQSxLUPBa8GhRomLD9hf6iRtFeXs8fcY) has worked on an [Ink! version](https://github.com/edgeware-builders/ink-atomic-swaps). It would be awesome if Edgeware integrates the pallet enabling a 'slow bridge' between KLP, Neatcoin and EDG. Note that Kulupu will integrate Paritytech's asset pallet and not Acala's [ORML pallet](https://github.com/open-web3-stack/open-runtime-module-library). Would this be a problem, I could ask to change this. Kulupu will also support the contracts pallet.

title: Lessons from Terra
body:
I've been following Terra Protocol ($LUNA) closely for some time. Like Edgeware, they are a new smart contract chain inside a multichain ecosystem. They also support WASM smart contracts, and support fair launches. Mirror, their synthetic assets protocol, was launched late last year with 100% of Mirror tokens being distributed to the community.

Unlike Edgeware, their base layer token $LUNA is used to mint a stablecoin called [TerraUSD](https://www.coingecko.com/en/coins/terra-usd), which uses a model similar to Basis. Also unlike Edgeware, they have raised a lot of money for the base layer, which is necessary because they have to stabilize the dollar and avoid the kinds of booms and crashes that have happened to [Empty Set Dollar](https://www.coingecko.com/en/coins/empty-set-dollar) or [Basis Cash](https://www.coingecko.com/en/coins/basis-cash).

Most interesting to me is that the Terra team is focused on building a platform for applications, rather than base layer development of the Cosmos SDK. **This is really similar to how we're not focused on core development of Substrate, and so, there are a lot of interesting lessons we could learn.**

My general takeaways are:

- You only need a handful of good applications to make a blockchain network feel like an active and exciting place. Terra has Mirror, Anchor, and a couple of others (payments rails that run on UST), and they are approaching a $10b market cap.
- dTrade might have the potential to become our Mirror — a real-world application which encourages people from outside the chain to come and lock up a large amount of assets. According to dTrade's website, there should be several forms of mining available to dTrade users, including [insurance mining, options mining and staking](https://dtrade.org/).

Hi folks, 
I was just thinking about how the community can respond to unforeseeable circumstances in a fast and efficient way through the governance system. 
Let's assume something happens and we need to push for a quick update in let's say within two weeks. What happens if a referendum about something else has just started which would prolong the waiting time another week.

title: Financing a working group for integrating Edgeware protocol into a DEX
body:
Hi all, 

with the Tokyo update around the corner which makes EDG attractive to Ethereum devs, it might be a good moment to think about a decentralised exchange(DEX) integration to Edgeware. To be clear not wrapped EDG listed on a Ethereum DEX but in fact a DEX running on Edgeware. 
There are several benefits for the Edgeware ecoystem:
0) More smart contracts on Edgeware, more fees, more staking reward. 
1) More ICOs or token would start on Edgeware as they would immediately have access to liquidity
2) More DAPPs would switch to Edgeware as they would not lose liquidity 
3) Many trading pairs for EDG which would create more values for the coin as bridging coin ( I always try to guess how much value of bitcoin or ethereum is only because its used for so many trading pairs and people need to buy it to buy something else)
4) Value locked in trading pairs on DEX 
5) Yield farming/Defi


What do you guys think, is this realistic, alined with the goals of the community and how could it be achieved? 
Several questions would need to be addressed:

1) How difficult is it given Tokyo upgrade and how long do you think it would take? 
2) How many devs should be involved, 
    can they be hired specifically to make the integration to Edgeware? If so one could open a Job advertisement
3) Funding allocation: 
    What would be a reasonable number of funding? 
    1 Million less or more? 
    Should it funded by the treasury and/or can the community even help to fund by contributing to the funding and is reward 
    with a fraction of the initial supply of the governance token? 
4) Would it be possible to contact existing protocol to collaborate which are at the moment solely running on Ethereum ? 
    Possible candidates: Uniswap, Sushishwap, LinkSwap, Bancor, Balancer, Cake etc. etc.

body:
So this is again a very hastily assembed agenda - apologies but here we go. I'm also going to experiment with noting call details into this post as we go.

This call again continues from the last three weeks where we covered:

1. Decent proposal - high level
2. Decent metaDAO - technical and governance aspects 
3. Decent partners - examples of potential groups who might be funded.


It's worth reiterating again that this proposal is still a work in progress and with hindsight I shouldn't have set specific deadlines for putting the proposal live since it left things feeling a little rushed. Per [the BuilDAO post](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/1091-rethinking-buildao-lessons-in-onchain-governance), the decisions made at the start of big initiatives cannot be unpicked... it's therefore incredibly important to be deliberate and cautious about decisions, even if there is a faster route to funding.

As we conduct these calls and more people get involved, new questions come up and I'm forced to better explain the core concepts - to people with varying levels of experience in crypto and who are interested in different aspects. This can be hard, but it forces me to constantly re-evaluate my arguments and to make better ones.

One big question that still remains and has been articulated by a few people is **"What does EDG get"?**

The concept of a metaDAO relies entirely on solving this Rubix cube - to give distinct advantages to individual chains, their token holders and cultures, whilst still remaining objectively independent.

title: Layer Wallet: an Edgeware mobile wallet
body:
The Edgeware ecosystem would benefit significantly from a high quality, open-source mobile wallet. There are a few ways we could implement one:

1. We could partner with an existing open-source wallet.
2. We could work with an independent developer to build a new wallet from scratch.
3. We could use exchange and blockchain partnerships to integrate with another ecosystem's wallet (e.g. partner with Sora → integrate with Fearless Wallet).


But each of these approaches involves a lot of uncertainty, management bandwidth, and time. Building a crypto wallet isn't technically an extremely hard problem, but making it fast, performant, and easy to use is difficult, and commissioning a wallet would usually require involving a long-term committed team with a high design bar, which is incredible challenging to do in crypto where the demand for that kind of team is overwhelming.

Finally, Edgeware has somewhat different needs that other networks:

- We aren't an interoperability network like Polkadot or Kusama, but an end-user facing network. While Kusama and Polkadot wallets are implementing WalletConnect, their timeline is stretched out far longer than ours.
- We aren't an EVM-on-Substrate platform like Moonbeam that can just fork existing Ethereum wallets.
- There are only a few good Polkadot ecosystem mobile wallets right now, and it's unclear what kind of support we will receive from them as we aren't a relay chain.


We are more focused on being a sovereign community-run network, so ideologically it makes sense to have an independent wallet that focuses on supporting Edgeware.

This thread proposes to fund and build Layer Wallet, a mobile wallet for the Edgeware ecosystem that prioritizes UX, simplicity, and extensibility.

title: Multichain Edgeware: A New Path to DOT
body:
Summary: This article describes an alternate path to the DOT ecosystem for Edgeware, and opens many other paths to value within the Edgeware network.

## Background

Recently, I [explored what a multichain Edgeware ecosystem might look like. ](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/1018-multiple-edgeware-chains-what-does-that-look-like) In order to make sense of this post, I encourage you to scan that one, as this is Part 2. 

Over the past months in discussion with community, ecosystem partners like CW Labs, and devs.. the opportunity to do something very different has become clear- and since we live on the EDG, I'm happy to advocate for some daring ideas today. I may mess a few things up myself in explaining- so take this all with a grain of salt, additionally..

The following _is a very early technological concept-_  we still have a lot of work to do validate the ideas I'm going to lay out here in a few parts:

## Background of The Relaychain Model and the Challenge

In the invention of Substrate and Polkadot, a core concept is that solo-chains become parachains. They 'share' their validation work, and therefore share the costs of network security. The inventor of the Polkadot model, Gavin Wood, has said that you can think of a relaychain like Polkadot like the United Nations: a collection of sovereign groups who come together for their common defense. 

However, the deployment of the relaychain has come with some surprise challenges in 'swapping' the operation of Edgeware Mainnet's consensus to the Polkadot side. Additionally, there are questions about what might happen if and when the chain ever decides to off-board from Polkadot- whether the chain would have to hard fork; something that we use on-chain upgrades and governance to avoid.
